Sir

Your Letters of the 15th & 19th Ins:t to the Board, have been read to them, as also your Letter to me.  Upon which they have commanded me to repeat to you their Acknowledgements & Thanks for you punctual Correspondance, and to acquaint you, that they have set all their Clerks at Work to copy the sev:l Papers in this Office, that may answer the several Queries you make in your Letter to me; But as they are pretty long & voluminous, I fear, it will be about this Day ten: night before they can be finished; However, no time shall be lost in the doing of it.  In the mean time, I am

Sir

Your most obedient & most humble Servant,
Wm Dopple 

Whitehall,
Janry 14th 1719/20

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
797.

Sir

Since our Letter to you, of the 21st: of last month, We have rec'd yours of 27th: Jan:ry  1:st, 3:d, 5:th, 10:th, 14:th & 22:d Instant N: S: for which and the Information you therein give Us, of the Mississippi Company, the Bank and of several other Matters, We return you Our hearty Acknowledgm:ts & Thanks.

Tho We did not expect you wou'd be able to give Us a particular Answer to the Quere We sent you in relation to the Duties payable in the Provinces not comprehended in the Tarif of 1664, because We find by Our Books, that those who made the Treaty of Commerce at Utrecht, were not able to do it; Yet as We apprehend that they did not take proper Methods to be sufficiently inform'd, We gave you the Trouble of that Inquiry.

We observe what you write in relation to the Hardships Our British Merchants complain of, which were in some Measure, tho not fully provided for by the Treaty of Commerce, & particularly that of the Droit d'Abêne; But We do not see, considering that the said Treaty has not yet had its Effect, what can be done at present.

We are very glad to have receiv'd from you the Copy of the Regent's Order for putting St: Lucia into the Condition it was in, before 

The Hon:ble
Daniel Pulteney

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
798.

before the Grant of it the Mareschal d'Estreé; But that Order was by the Informations We have had, leave about 50 French families settled there, & may in time give the French a pretence to claim a Right by possession, and make that one of their Droits incontestables; However, if the French Commissaries have given you any Deduction of their Title to that Island, We shall be oblig'd to you for an Account of it.

We were in hopes to have heard from you that the Conference with the French Commissaries upon the other matters, which you were impower'd to treat as had been renew'd and shall always very thankfully receive what Information you shall give Us upon those or any other Matters; We are,

Sir,

Your most Obedient & most humble Servants,

Westmorland
J. Chetwynd
Charles Cooke
C. Docminique
J. Molesworth
T. Pelham
Martin Bladen

Whitehal,
Febr:y 23:d 1719/20

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
801. 805

Sir

I am honour'd with yours of 12th Inst: N: S: and am to acquaint You, that the Board are very well satisfied with the Information You give them in relation to the Duties that were paid in the Provinces not comprehended in the Tariff of 1664, and therefore what they writ You in their Letter of 23:d of last Month, was only to give You the Reasons for their having made  that Enquiry, & not that they intended to give You any further Trouble upon that Matter; However they would be very glad if You could procure them the Tariff of 1667, which they have not. 

There have of late been several Complaints exhibited against Mr. Lowther, two of which were referr'd to this Board relating to his taking Presents to the Value of £23,000 and upwards, and to his admitting a Spanish Ship to trade at Barbados, contrary to the Acts of Trade; Both which Articles have appear'd plainly to the Board from the Minutes of Council & Assembly, & his own Letters; so that a Representation has been made, stating the Facts as they appear'd to
the

The Hon:ble Dan. Pulteney, Esqr

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
800. 802.

the Board.  Several other Complaints against him have been heard  before the Lords of the Committee of Council, which have been to his Disadvantage, so that it is expected he will soon be recalled.

The Board having made further Enquiry in relation to S:ta Lucia, have received two Papers whereof the inclosed are Copies from Mr. Sharpe, late President of the Council of Barbados, and Mr. Gordon, whom You know.  These were in Answer to the Queries You made some time ago in a Letter to me.  I am, 

Sir,

Your most Obedient and most humble Servant,

Wm Dopple

P:S:  Since the writing of this, I have in an old Book found the printed Tariff of 1667, so that You need not be at the trouble of sending it.

The inclos'd Pamphlet was given by Mr. Gec, to Board.

WD

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
805

Sir,

His Majesty having been pleas'd to refer to Us an Address of the House of Commons, (a Copy whereof is here inclos'd) relating to proper Methods for preventing the running of Wooll from Great Britain & Ireland into foreign Parts, We are taking all the necessary Measures to be thoroughly appriz'd of the several Abuses committed therein, And as this is of Importance to Great Britain, We intreat you to give your Self the Trouble of enquiring, as well as you are able, into all Matters relating to this affair, & of communicating to Us what Informations you can obtain thereupon.

We are,  

Sir,

Your most obedient humble Servant,

Westmorland

Charles Cooke
C. Docminique
T. Pelham

Whitehall,
July y:e 1:st 1720

Hon:ble Dan:l Pulteney, Esq:re

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
807.

Jovis, 5. die May 1720

Resolv'd, Nemine Contradicente, That an Humble Address be presented to His Majesty, That he wil be graciously pleas'd to issue his Royal Proclamation, promising such further Reward as he shall think fit for the discovering any Person or Persons that shall run or export Wooll or Woollen Yarn, until further Provision shall be made by Parliament for preventing the same ; And that His Majesty will further be graciously pleas'd to order the Commissioners of Trade & Plantations, during the Recess of Parliament, to consider of, & lay before His Majesty, & both Houses of Parliament, at the beginning of the next Session of Parliament what they shall find further necessary to be done to prevent that pernicious Practice of runing Wooll from Great Britain & Ireland into Foreign parts, which is so destructive to the Woollen Manufactures of this Kingdom.

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
813.

Sir

I have spoke to the Board about what you write in your Letter of the 17th Aug:t N.S. in relation to Judge Conservadors in Spain, but they have been in such a Hurry occasion'd by so many different References from us Lords Justices which requir'd immediate Dispatch that they have not been able to consider what you propose, so as to direct me to give you an Answer, particularly they were requir'd to prepare a Commission & Instructions for a Governor of Carolina under the King, & withal to propose what might be reasonable & necessary for securing our Frontiers in those parts ag:t the French on Mississipi, who as tis rumour'd here are endeavouring to make a Settlem:t upon the River St: Mathco on the Eastern Coast of Florida, between St: Augustine & Carolina which will be, if effected, of dangerous Consequence to all our Plantations.  The Representation that went with the Instructions was  but provisional till the main Report upon all the Plantations can be finish'd.  However as there are several things in it worth Notice I send you a Copy thereof here inclosed.  When the gen:l Representation

is

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
814.

is done (which I cannot foresee will be in a little time) I will send you also a Copy of it.

There are no Answers to the Queries sent to the Governors, but what you saw when you went from hence, particularly Mr. Keith's Answer.  But upon this Occasion the Board have given the same Queries but with some Additions to several Persons here.  Some of them have return'd Answers, & others not, as soon as I get a spare Hand.  You shall be sure to have Copies of them as they come.

I have receiv'd Edicts Arrêts or Regulations mention'd in your several Letters and particularly in that of the 3:d Sept:r N.S. with the Code Marin for which the Board command we to return you their hearty Thanks.  

I had forgot to tell you that the Lords Justices have agreed to what is propos'd in the foremention'd Rep:ts relating to Carolina, and have sent it to his Ma:ty for his Approbation.  Upon this Occasion they have requir'd the Board to lay before them a Representation of what may be necessary to the Bahama Islands.

They

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
815.

They have nam'd General Nicholson for Governor of Carolina, which is a Surprise to every Body that has heard it.  He seems to be too old for such an Undertaking, besides, the Settlem:t of this Colony at present requires a Man of Temper and Understanding, Such a One as Col. Hart who is lately arriv'd from Maryland, who had been recommended to the Lords Justices for that Employment, but Gen:l Nicholson has got it.  I am

Sirs 

Your most obedient & most humble Serv:t
Wm Dopple 

Whitehall
Sept:r 8th 1720

P.S. I have just now rec'd your Letter of the 10:th Ins:t but it is impossible by this Messenger to answer what you desire, but I will do it very plainly I hope by Monday.  In the mean time I am very sure that the french Fishery at Canço was upon the Continent of Nova Scotia; But in case it had been upon the small Isl:ds thereto adjacent, they are within the Limits from w:ch the French are excluded by y:r Treaty.

WD

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
817.

Sir,

I have receiv'd the Hon:r of your Letter of the 5th Ins:t N: S: I observe what you say about the Island of Canço.  Tis certain that those little Rocks or Islands mention'd by Gaughan & Capon lye but at a very small Distance from the Continent, yet Boats and small Craft may pass between the Cape and them.  However they are certainly within the Limits assign'd to us by the Treaty.

  Mr. Cumings having presented to the Board an Extract of a Letter he had receiv'd from Cap:t Southack in New England giving an acco:t, that some French with their Indians had this year interrupted Our fishing at Canço & seiz'd to the Value of about ten thousand pounds British Effects &c:a.  The Board immediately made a Representation thereupon (Copies of both which are here inclos'd for your Information).

Upon this Occasion Mr. Cumings acquainted the Board that there is now in Town a LIeu:t of a Man of War who had been several times at Cape Canço and the Islands contiguous to it, & that he had made himself, whilst he was there particular Dra:ts of that part of the Country, which Dra:ts that Gentleman brought to the Board the

Day

Hon:ble Mr. Pulteney

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
818.

Day after, & the Substance of what he said was to the same Purpose as what is mentioned in the first parag of this Letter.

The Board have receiv'd a Letter from Col. Philips, dated at Annapolis the 26th May last, & a Duplicate being come of the said Letter & all the Papers therein referr'd to, I thought it wou'd not be unacceptable to you to send you the said Duplicates which are here inclos'd.

There have been several Hearings before the Lords Justices in Council upon Complaint against Mr. Lowther for very high Crimes, and the Complainants have fully made out every Article against him, They are to go on, on Tuesday next on other Articles.  I am  

Sir,

Your most obedient and most humble Servant,

Wm Dopple

Whitehall
Oct:r ye 20th: 1720

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
821.

Sir

Having nothing to communicate to you from the Board, I am only to acknowledge the Receipt of Your Letter of the 11:th of Novem:r N:S:, and to acquaint you, that according to Your Desire I have writ to the several Governors for an Answer to the Queries mention'd in Your Letter.  I am

Sir

Your most Obedient & most humble Servant,

Wm Dopple

Whitehal
Nov:r y 10:th 1720.

Sir

The Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations command me to send you the inclos'd Copy of a Map of Canço Harbour drawn by Cap:t Young upon the Place which he did for his own Use without any View to the Disputes between France and Us. And therefore it is to be suppose'd that he has done it without Partiality.  I am

Sir

Your most Obedient & most humble Servant
Wm Dopple

Whitehal.
Novem:r y 24:th 1720.

The Hon:ble Mr. Pulteney.

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
829.

Sir

The Lords Commiss:rs for Trade & Plantations have commanded me to return you their hearty Thanks and Acknowledgments for your Letter of 25th last Month N:S:, relating to the running of Wooll, and they easily conceive. that it is very difficult for you to get any better Information than what you have sent them.

In relation to the Business of Canço mention'd in your Letter to me of y:e 5th of the last Month N:S: I have only to add to my former Letters, that by all the Acco:ts the Board have had, it appears that the French have fish'd not only upon the Islands, but upon Cape Canço it Self.

Since my last Letter, Cap. Young the Lieu:te of the Man of War mention'd therein has given to the Board a Mem:l in Writing, a Copy whereof is here inclos'd for you Information, and tho it does not come up to what you desire, yet there may be some things in that you'd be glad to know.  I am

Sir

Your most obed:t and most humble Servant
Wm Dopple

Whitehall
Nov:r y:e 3d 1720

Hon:ble Dan:l Pulteney Esq:r

P.S.

Gentlemen,

We have receiv'd Mr. Blanden's Letter of the 11th Inst: N: P: with the Copy of his Memorial, relating to Hudson's Bay, to which we have no Objection.

We have also receiv'd a Letter from Mr. Delafaye by Order of the Lords Justices, relating to that Article of your Instructions, which requires you to correspond with Us &c: a Copy whereof is here inclos'd for your Information.

There is one thing in which we must desire your Assistance, and is as follows,
By the 9th Article of the Treaty of Comerce with France at Utrecht, it is provided, "That the Duties payable in France by the Subjects of Great Britain for Goods Imported and Exported, shall be paid according to the Tenour of the Tarif of 1664, and shall not exceed the Rule therein settled in the provinces, whereof mention is there made, and in the other Provinces the Duty shall not be payable otherwise than according to the Rule at that time prescrib'd."  Upon which the following Query has arisen; By what Rule or Rules were the Duties paid in the several Provinces of France, that were not comprehended in the Tarif.

The Hon:ble Dan'l Pulteney & Martin Bladen Esq:s

Instructions for Daniel Pulteney and Martin Bladen Esq:s appointed His Majesty's Commissaries to treat with the Commissary or Commissaries to be appointed by the Most Christian King.  Given at Whitehal Septem:r 3rd 1719.  In the 6th Year of His Majesty's Reign.

Together with these Instructions you will receive His Majesty's Commission under the Great Seal of Great Britain appointing you the said Daniel Pulteney and Martin Bladen joyntly and severally to be his Majesty's Commissaries for treating of and concluding with the Commissary or Commissaries on the part of the French King all such Matters and Things as are referr'd to Your Cognizance & Determination by the said Commission, in pursuance of the 10th: 11th: 12th: 13th: 14th: and 15th: Articles of the Treaty of Peace concluded at Utrecht the 31 Day of March/April in the Year of Our Lord 1713 between Her late Majesty Queen Anne & Lewis the 14th late the most Christian King.

You are therefore with all convenient Speed to repair to the French Court where you are to meet the Commissary or Commissaries to

be

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
730.

be appointed by the Most Christian King to whom you shall communicate your full powers, and at the  same time inspect the Commission or powers given to him or them in order to see whether they be in due and sufficient form, in which Case You are to enter into Treaty with the said Commissary or Commissaries, wherein you shall proceed, as directed by Your Commission & these Instruct:ns.

It being provided by the 10th Article of the Treaty of Utrecht that the Limits & Boundaries between Hudsons Bay and the places appertaining to the French be settled by Commissaries on each part, which Limits both the British & French Subjects shall be wholly forbid to pass over, or thereby to go to each other by Sea or by Land.  You are to endeavour to get the said Limits settled in the following manner, That is to say,

That the same begin from the Island call'd Grimington's Island or Cape Perdrix in the Latitude of 58½ North, which 
the Company desire may be the Boundary between the British & French Subjects on the Coast of Laboradore towards Rupert's Land on the East Main & Nova Britannia on the French Side, and that no French Ship, Banque; Boat or Vessel whatsoever shall pass to the North Westward of Cape Perdrix or Grimington's Island towards

or

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
731

or unto the Streights or Bay of Hudson on any pretence whatsoever.  And further that a Line be drawn from the South Westward of the Island of Grinington or Cape Perdrix (so as to include the same within the Limits of the Bay) to the great Lake Miscosinke als[[?]] Mistoveny dividing the said Lake into two parts (as in the Map to be deliver'd to you.)  And that where the said Line shall cut the 49th Degree of Northern Latitude, another Line shall begin and be extended Westward from the said Lake upon the 49th Degree of Northern Latitude, over which said Lines so to be describ'd as above mention'd the French and all persons by them imploy'd shall be prohibited to pass to the Northward of the said 49th Degree of Latitude and to the North or Northwestward of the said Lake or suppos'd Line by Land or Water on or through any Rivers, Lakes or Countries to trade or erect any Forts or Settlements; And the British Subjects shall likewise be forbid to pass the said suppos'd Line either to the Southward or Eastward.  But you are to take especial Care in wording such Articles as shall be agreed on with the Commissary or Commissaries of His Most Christian Majesty upon this Head, that the said Boundaries be understood to regard the Trade of the Hudson's Bay Company only; That His Majesty does not thereby recede from His Right to any Lands in America not compriz'd within the said Boundaries & that no pretensions be thereby given to the French to claim any

Tracts

Tracts of Land in America Southward or Southwest of the said Boundaries.

 And whereas it hath been represented by the said Company, That the French have since the peace at Utrecht Viz in 1715, made a Settlement at the Head of Albany River, upon which River the Company's principal Factory is settled whereby the French may intercept the Indian Trade from coming to the said Factory, and may in time utterly ruin the Trade of the Company, if not prevented.  You are to insist that the said Fort be given up or demolish'd by the French and their Subjects withdrawn from that Settlement.

Ane it being further provided by the 11th Article of the said Treaty that Satisfaction be made according to Justice & Equity to the Hudson's Bay Company for the Damages & Spoil done to their Colonies, Ships, persons & Goods by the hostile Incursions & Depredations of the French in time of peace.  And the said Company having deliver'd to His Maj:t's Commiss:rs for Trade & plantations an Account under their Common Seal of the Losses sustain'd by them from the French in time of peace, which will be deliver'd to you with proper Vouchers for the same.  You are in like manner to insist that Satisfaction be made to the Company, pursuant to the said Article.

And

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
733.

And whereas by the 12th Article of the said Treaty, Nova Scotia or Accadie with its ancient Boundaries as also the City of Port Royal now call'd Annapolis Royal, and all other Things in those parts which depend on the said Lands & Islands, together with the Dominion propriety & possession of the said Lands, Islands &  places.  And all Right whatsoever by Treaties or by any other way obtain'd which the Most Christian King, the Crown of France or any the Subjects thereof have hitherto had to the said Lands, Islands & places, and the Inhabitants of the same were yielded & made over to the late Queen and to the Crown of Great Britain forever.  Except Cape Breton & the other Islands lying in the Mouth of the River of St. Laurence and in the Gulph of the same Name.  You are to take Notice that the Boundaries of Nova Scotia are describ'd by the Charter of King James the 1st to Sir William Alexander afterwards Earl of Sterling, bearing Date the 10th of Septem:r 1621 in the following Words Viz: "All the Lands & Islands lying within the promontory commonly call'd Cape Sables being in the 43rd Degree of North Latitude or thereabouts, thence Westerly to the Bay commonly call'd St. Mary's Bay & from thence Northerly in a Streight Line by the Mouth of that Great Bay (which runs Easterly up the Country & divides the two Nations call'd Surriquois & Pechmines) to the River St. Crois thence Westerly to the Head of that River, thence Northerly to the next Bay, which discharges

it

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
"itself in the River St. Laurence thence Easterly along the Coast to the Bay of Gaspe, thence South Easterly to the Bacalio Isl: or Cape Breton, and leaving those Islands on the Right, and the Gulph of St. Laurence & Newfoundland & the Islands thereto belonging upon the left thence to Cape Breton in the Latitude of 45 Degrees or there abouts then South West to Cape Sables again.

But whereas in Consequence of the Treaty of Breda several other Lands were formerly deliver'd up by Sir Tho. Temple as part of Nova Scotia to the French, which Lands did belong to the Crown of Great Britain, altho they were not a part of Nova Scotia.  Since which time the French in Consequence of that Cession did make several Settlements upon the said Lands & others belonging likewise to the Crown of Great Britain, lying Westward & South Westward of Nova Scotia between the River of St. Laurence & Atlantick Ocean & did annex the same to Nova Scotia as appears by a Commission given by the late French King to Mr. Subercaic where he is term'd Governor of Accadie & Cape Breton Island & Islands adjacent from Cape Rosiers of the great River St. Laurence, as far as the East part of Kennebeck River; Now You are to insist that the French are oblig'd by the Treaty of Utrecht to deliver up all 

Lands

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
735.

Lands and Settlements whatever which they have at any time possess'd as part of or dependent on Nova Scotia, and that His Most Christian Majesty has no Right to any Lands whatever lying between the said River of St. Laurence and the Atlantic Ocean except such Islands as lye in the Mouth of the said River and in the Gulph of St. Laurence, and are given up to the French by the Treaty of Utrecht; Wherefore You are to press that the necessary Orders be dispatch'd for the due Execution of this Article of the Treaty which hath not hitherto been fully comply'd with.

And whereas the French have for several Years since the Conclusion of the last peace taken upon them not only to fish on the Coast of Nova Scotia & on the Islands of Canceau, but likewise to make Settlements on the said Islands, Notwithstanding they are expressly prohibited by the 12th Article of the Treaty of Utrecht from fishing in any of the Seas, Bays & other places on the Coast of Nova Scotia that is to say, on those which lye towards the South East within thirty Leagues beginning from the Isl: commonly call'd Sable inclusive and thence stretching along towards the South West; You are hereby directed to insist that the French have no Right or Title to fish any where within 30 Leagues of the South East Coast of Nova Scotia beginning from the Island of Sable inclusively & thence stretching along to the 

South

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
736.

South West, or to fish or make any Settlements on the Islands of Canceau or any other Islands within the Gut or Bay of the same Name, which belong to His Maj:ty as  part of Nova Scotia, nothing being reserv'd to the French by the said Treaty except Cape Breton and the Islands lying within the Mouth of the River of St. Laurence or the Gulph of the same Name.  But if the French Commissary or Commissaries shou'd pretend to ground a more extensive Claim upon the Words of the said Treaty as it was sign'd in French than does appertain to them by the same Treaty as it was sign'd in Latin, You are to insist upon it that the Treaty in Latin is to be Your Guide in all Cases tho even by the Treaty in French they can have no Title to any Islands lying in the Bay or Gut of Canceau.

And whereas by the 14th Article of the said Treaty.  It is expressly provided that in all the said places & Colonies to be yielded & restor'd by the Most Christian King in pursuance of the said Treaty the Subjects of the said King may have Liberty to remove themselves within a Year to any other place together with all their movable Effects.  You are to take Notice that the French Inhabit: of Nova Scotia have long since elaps'd the Time for removing their persons & Effects from thence, And are thereby absolutely 

be

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
737.

become Subjects to the Crown of Great Britain.  And whereas they have hitherto refus'd to take the Oaths of Fidelity & Allegiance to His Maj:ty or to the late Queen being instigated thereunto by their priests & even by the Governors of Quebec and of Cape Breton.  As the Indians have also been to set up a Claim to all that Country, You are to use your utmost Endeavours to obtain a particular Order from the French Court requiring the said Governors of Quebec & Cape Breton and the Missionaries in those parts for the future not to interpose or meddle with any thing that does or may concern His Majesty's Interest in Nova Scotia, and particularly that they do not dissuade His Majesty's French Subjects there from taking the Paths of Fidelity & Allegiance to His Majesty, nor instigate the Indians to molest or disturb His Majesty's Subjects in those parts.

Whereas upon Application made by the French Court, We did lately cause Restitution to be made to Mons:r Hiriberry of a Ship taken off the Coast of Canceau by the Squirrel Man of War upon Assurance given by the French Minister residing here, that Orders had then been given by the French Court for Restitution to be made to His Majesty's Subjects of all such Ships or Effects as had been taken by the French by Way of Reprizal upon that account now in Case the said Restitution shall not have been made.  You are to insist that effectual Orders

be

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722
transcription:
738.

be given by the French Court for that purpose without further Delay. And at the same time you will take notice that this Reprizal was made directly contrary to the 16th Article of the Treaty of Utrecht.

It being especially provided by the 13th Article of the Treaty of Utrecht that after the Cession of Newfoundland made by His Most Christian Majesty, His Subjects shou'd not fish upon any part of the Coasts of the said Island except only from Cape Bonavista to the Northern point of the said Island, and from thence running down by the Western Side to Pointe  Riche.  Notwithstanding which provision, It has been represented that the French have sometimes taken upon them to fish on other parts of the said Island contrary to the express Words of the aforesaid Article.  You are to insist that the French Court do give strict Orders for the more punctual Observance thereof for the future.

Whereas the 5 Nations of Indians bordering upon New York are undoubtedly subject to the Crown of Great Britain whose Right of Dominion over them is fully acknowledg'd by the 15th Article of the said Treaty.  Now you are hereby directed to endeavour to procure an Order to the Gov:r of Canada & of Cape Breton requiring them in the strongest Terms not to molest or disturb

nor

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722

nor to suffer the Indians in Alliance with the French to molest or disturb in any manner the said 5 Indian Nations.  Directing likewise them the said Governors and each of them to recall the Missionaries now settled among the said 5 Indian Nations, and not to permit any other Missionaries to go amongst them for the future upon any pretence whatsoever.

Whereas it is provided by the 11th Article of the said Treaty, that Satisfaction shall be made for all Ships or Goods taken by the Subjects of either Nation from the other in time of peace; You are hereby requir'd to insist that Satisfaction be made accordingly to such of His Majesty's Subjects whose Claims & Demands upon this Head shall be deliver'd to you herewith or transmitted to you hereafter, during the Course of Your Negotiation; But no Application having hitherto been made by the French Court to His Maj:ty concerning any Damage of this Nature sustain'd by their Subjects, if the Commissary or Commissaries of His most Christian Majesty shou'd demand Reparation for any Ships or Goods taken from the French in time of peace; before you enter into the Discussion of such Demands, You are to send home Copies of the several Cases to one of His Majesty's principal Secretaries of State, or to Our Secretary, during His Majesty's Absence in order to obtain full Information thereof from hence and to give the parties concern'd in Great Britain an Opportunity of making their Answer thereunto.

In relation to the French Settlements at Missisippi, Mr. Bath said, that he had liv’d among the Indians (with 6 or 7 white people which he had brought with him as Servts) on Cusaw River about 700 Miles from Charles Town; That several hundreds of the English of Carolina traded there; That the French had a Settlement upon the same River, but nearer to the Sea, That  the English had traded with the Indians above 30 Years. Capn Reed said, that to his Knowledge the River Potomac in Maryland was navigable for above 150 Miles up into the Country, and that he had been inform’d some had said up for above 200 Miles, and that there it was not fordable; That the Virginians being at Enmity with the Indians have given 5 £ a head for every Indian that was kill’d; That the Reason why the Indians won’t be friends with the Virginians is because they don’t make any acknowledgment to them for the Land they take up, That the People in Maryland were always Friends with the Indians, That some of their Indians proferr’d to carry some English to the French Settlement from the Indians Settlement on MIssisippi in two Days; That the Indians never settle long in a place, as soon as the Land where they settled is worn out, they remove to another.

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [5], 1717-1722

Mr. Danson being ask’d how far Westward the people of Carolina understood their Boundaries to extend, he said they extended westward as far as the ocean, and that they traded with all the Indians that way, but that they had no forts that way at all.

Mr. Colmer said that Mr. Laws told him he had been inform’d the French had already sent 8000 Negroes to Missisippi.

Mr Byth being desir’d by the Board to put into Writing what he had to offer in relation to the several matters he had spoke of to the Board, he promis’d to do it.

Propositions and Considerations for the Business of Canada

The Kings Majesty's Interest of Right of Title to Laradia, Canada, & the Countrys adjacent is derived from the time that Sebastian Cabott tempore Hen:7 took possession of that Continent, & those Countrys for the Crown of Eng. as the first Discoverer. And for the Gulf, & River of Canada (where the French lately planted) it is confessed by them in their Mayor that it was first discovered by the English. The Interest of this State for the possessing & planting those Countrys is, That the Gulf & River of Canada, the Bay of Playfance [?], & the Sea Coast adjacent are the cheif places, & so by Consequence the sole Nursery, & Means to increase Shipping, & Marriners for France, & Spain, (1000 French Marriners were taken Prisoners there by the English the last year) & also the transporting of Fish from thence into the Streights, Barbary, & Spain enricheth them with much Treasure. Another Interest of State is That by the possession of Lacadia, Nova Scotia, the Gulf & the River of Canada, & parts adjacent (to which the French pretendeth.) The King shall be sole Master of all that Continent from Virginia to Newfoundland, which is of a very considerable consequence, for the Trade of Furrs, & other good Merchantable Commodities; for Fishing, increase of Shipping, & Marriners, & the Hopes of furnishing his Majestys Shore-Houses from the River & Gulf of Canada with Masts, pitch, tar, & other materials & provisions for Shipping, & by the French Interest in those parts the King's plantations & profits in those several considerations will receive Prejudice & Interruption Divers English Merchants & others the last Year, during the War with France, set out certain ships under the Command of Capt. Keirk with great Costs & Charges into those parts, & their Voyage succeeded so well, that they took possession of the Gulf & the greatest part of the River of Canada, (which the French for this 24 or 25 years last past have usurped) & took down the French Arms, which were planted at a place called Tatousask [?], & set up the English arms in their place. Immediately about the time that Columbus discovered the Isle of Cuba, Sebastian Cabott set out from England by Hen: 7th did first discover the Continent of America, beginning at Newfoundland & there after going to the Gulf of Canada, & from thence having seen Cape Breton all along the Coast to Florida by which discovery his Majesty hath the Title to Virginia, New England & New Scotland as being then first discovered by Cabott at the Charge of the King of England. The French after this neglecting the Knowledge thereof by Jacques Cartier of the River of Canada as a Cold Climate or as it may be in regard it was challenged as first discovered by the English having a great desire to possess themselves in some parts of America

They planted first a Colony under the Charge of Monsr. Villegagnon in Brasil & another under the Charge of Monsr. Laudoniere in Florida from both which they were expelled by the Spaniards.

When giving over all hopes of attempting any thing that did belong to the Spaniards & pushing by all means to have some Interest in America notwithstanding that the English (altho’ they were not able to possess all at first) had possessed them of that Continent or discovered by them by a Colony in the South part thereof now called Virginia & by another in the North part thereof now called New England & New Scotland planted by Justice Popham.

The French in the time of Hen: 4th under the Charge of Monsr. Poutrincourt having seen all the Coast of New England & New Scotland to both which parts they did then begin to claim Right they seated themselves in Port Royal out of which as soon as it was made known to the English they were displaced by S. Sam. Argall as having wrongfully intruded themselves within those Bounds which did belong to this Crown both by Discovery & possession.

The remainder of this French Colony not having occasion to be transported to France stayed still in the Country yet they were so neglected by the State not owning them any more & hardly supplyed in that which was necessary for them by voluntary Adventurers who came to trade in hope of their Commodities in Exchange of what they brought & during the time of King James there was no Complaint made upon S. Sam. Argall for having displaced them & they were now lately glad to demand that protection from his Majesty which was not offered them from any other whereby it may evidently appear that his Majesties Title was thought good otherwise it was likely that the French King if any wrong had been done unto him would have sought to have had the same repaired, either by Treaty or otherwise. But without either making any private Complaint, or yet doing any publick Act against the same they went next & erected themselves upon the North side of the River

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [4], 1717-1722
transcription:
River of Canada at Quebeck a place whereunto the English by a preceding Title might likewise have claimed right, but small notice was taken thereof till during the time of the late War a Command was given by his Majesty to remove them from thence which was accordingly performed the place being taken a little after the peace was concluded which at that time had not come to the takers knowledge & a Colony of Scottish was planted at Port Royal which had never been repossessed nor claimed by the French since they were first removed from thence.

This Business of Port Royal cannot be made liable to the Articles of Peace seeing there was no Act of Hostility committed thereby a Colony only being planted upon his Majesty’s own ground according to a Patent granted by his Majesty’s late dear Father & his Majesty’s self having as good Right thereunto as to any part of that Continent & the possession taken thereupon was in the time of his Majesty’s dear Father as it is set down at length in the Voyages written by Pureas but neither by that possession nor the subsequent plantation hath any thing been taken from the French whereof they had any Right at all or yet any possession for the time & what might have been done either before the War without a breach of Peace cannot justly be complained upon for being done at that time.

After that the Scotch Colony was planted at Port Royal they & the French who dwell there having met with the Commanders of the Natives called by them Sagamores did make choice of one of the chiefest of them called Sagamo Sigipt [[?]] to come in the name of the rest to his Majesty for acknowledging of his Title & to become his Majesty’s Subjects craving only to be protected by his Majesty against their Enemies which demand of his was accepted by his Majesty who did promise to protect them as he reported to the rest at his return.

Mons. Le tour who was chief Commander of the few French then in that Country being neglected as is said by his own Country men & finding his Majesty’s Title not so much as questioned after their being expelled from Port Royal & the coming in of the Scotch necessary for his Security did come along with the same Sagamo [[?]] & demanding the like in the Name of the French who live there so that his Majesty hath a good Right to New Scotland by Discovery by possession of his Majesty’s Subjects by removing the French who had seated themselves at Port Royal & by Mons. Le tour the Commander of them there his turning Tenant & by the voluntarily turning Tenants of

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [4], 1717-1722
transcription:
the rest to his Majesty. And that no Obstacle might remain the very Savages by their own willingly offering their Obedience to his Majesty so that his Majesty is now bound in honour to maintain them both in regard of his Subjects that have planted there upon his Warrant & the promise he made unto the Commrs.[?] of the Natives that came to him from thence.

French Ambassador’s Memorial concerning L’Acadia

In the Year 1628 the French King granted the Province of L’Acadie to the Company of New France forbidding in the said Grant all Persons of what quality soever to traffick with the Savages by way of Truck for Skins which is all the Product & Commerce of that Country. In 1657 the Company of New France nominated unto the King Seire Le Bourgne to be Governour of the said Province whereupon the King gave him a Commission to command those in that Quality & renewed his Prohibitions concerning the traffick & Truck aforementioned. Contrary whereunto an English Bark of 15 or 16 Tun (in Augst 1661) was met with in the Port of Lahave (which is in the midst of the said Province) laden with 200 Beavers & 60 other Skins gotten by trucking & with other Commodities intended for the continuance of that traffick in this condition the Vessel was taken by the said Seire Le Bourgne his Son Lieutenant in his Father’s absence & thence brought into France where the Court of Admiralty desiring to proceed against 7[?] of the Ships Company according to the extremity of the Laws & to that end having imprisoned them the said Seire Le Bourgne consented to their enlargement whereupon they were set at Liberty.

The said Seire Le Bourgne being now in London by Order from the King in the French Ambassadors family to waite an Issue of his solicitations with the K. of Gr. Britain for restitution of a part of L’Acadie usurped by the English under an illegal Government & upon a pretence of a surreptitious Grant from Oliver Cromwell against all right, Seire Bataille Secretary of the French Embassy doth in his Ambassadors absence desire That seeing the Justification of the said prize depends upon that Regulation which is expected concerning the said restitution The King of Gr. Britain would be pleased in the mean time to suspend & surcease all Orders that may be required against the said Seire Le Bourgne by the Owners of the foresaid Bark forasmuch also as he offers to give Security not only to the value of the said prize but of all other taken by the French from the English as offenders against the foresaid Prohibitions in case the said restitution be not adjudged to be made. Provided that at the same time those that shall appear as Parties do offer & do the like for the prizes which will be proved to have been unduly taken from

transcription:
547
May it please yor Lordships
I hold it my Duty to acquaint you that I received his Majesty's Letter Dated the 31st of Decem. 1667 for the delivering up of the Country of Acadia the 20th of Oct. 1668 by Mons de Morillon du Bourg deputed by the most Christian King under the great Seal of France to receive the same to whom I returned my Answer a Copy of which under his Hand & Seal I have here enclosed to which I humbly refer yor Lordships.
The 10th of Novr instant I rec'd his Majesty's Letter dated the first of Augst commanding me not to deliver up the Country until his further pleasure was known which I shewed the said Mons Du Bourg I thought fit also to let yor Lordships know that those parts & places named in my first Order were a part of one of the Colonies of New England viz pentagost belonging to New Plimouth while hath given the Magistrates here great Cause of fear & apprehensions of so potent a Neighbor which may be of dangerous consequence to his Majesty's Service & Subjects; the Caribbee Islands having most of their provisions from these parts and the more since the Mons informs me that the most Christian King intended to plant a Colony at Pentagost & make a passage by Land to Quebeck his greatest Town in Canada being but 3 days Journey distant.
I humbly beseech your Lordship's pardon if I presume to inform you that Acadia is but a small part of Nova Scotia being the first National patent regularly bounded in all America limited on the North by the great River of Canada & on the West with New England containing the two large provinces of Alexandria & Caledonia established & confirmed by divers Acts of Parliament in Scotland & annexed to the Crown the Recods where of are kept in the Castle of Edinburgh to this day, a Country that might be of infinite advantage to his Majesty & Subjects were it improved abounding in good Harbours Rivers good Land Mines excellent Timber of all sorts especially for Shipping & the Seas abounding with Cod Fish the only Revenue at present fit being unpeopled is made by Furrs & Elk skins to the value of 900 Ann. of which Mr Elliot receives 600. I had made a beginning to set up a fishing Trade about 3 years since as yor Lordships may see if you please to cast your Eyes on these few prints inclosed but the War then breaking forth dashed it wholy & caused the French my neighbours to make divers attempts upon the Country under my Command which through God's blessing on my Endeavours I preserved at my own proper Cost & Charges having not

Right Honble:

In Obedience to your Lordshp Comands I herein give my Opinion of the Sea Coast of Nova Scotia from Cape Sables whose Latitude is 43°:30°: North to Cape Canso Lat 45°:40° Distant about 80 Leagues, the Country within Hight & Mountaneous, the Water Side plain even Arable Land fit for planting great Quantities of fine Oak & the very best Masts for the Navy and a fishery beyond Newfoundland in every Degree From One Mile of the Shore to 20 Leagues into the Sea.
Many Excellent Harbours for Ships
Port Roseway, Port Mattone, Matway La Have, Shebouchter, Shedore, Liscomb Harbour, Country Harbour, Tangier, Torbay Isaac Harbour, But what excels them all is Canso wch is invaluable for it fishery. Tis here such great Quantities of Cod, Herring & Mackerel swarm amongst the Islands that when I was there in His Majt's Ship [[?]] there was then 96 Sail of English & 200 french making their Voyages the English Vessels from 50 to 70 Tuns the french small shallops, And when fish is scarce at other places, here they are
always

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [4], 1717-1722
transcription:
504.

always plenty for on letting the Line down they draw up Two & Two as fast as they can pull it.

Upon my arrival at Canso having serv’d the French was come over with a Design to fish, I order’d them away to their own Coast And after went with His Maj Ship to Louisburgh where Monsr St Avi[[?]] Brovilliard the then Governor assur’d me he knew nothing of those fishermens going over for that ‘twas contrary to the Treaty of Peace, and that he shou’d take Caution to prevent their doing the like for the future. I sail’d again to Canso where Our Vessels were all soon laden, I now thereby leave to acquaint Your Lordshp: that when a Ship of War is not there or anything to hinder the French fishing among us that then Our fishing Vessels cannot take 4 fish when they will take Ten. They fish with Fresh & [[?]] with Salt Bait. We come 180 Leagues they but Seven. They in small Boats, We in large Sloops, all which is for want of a Garrison or a protection of Our People from the Indians who the French set on to Our Ruin the those parts.

If a fort were to be built King George Island formerly call’d Canso Island wou’d be

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [4], 1717-1722
transcription:
be the best place which Fortification wou'd command the Harbour all the Entrances into it the Beaches where the fishermen cure their Fish & prevent the French or Indians from disturbing Us, A Ship of War must attend this Work till it's completed which wherever they appear in the Plantations carrys Awe to the French & Dread to the Indians
I must humbly beg your Lord's Favour, if there is a small ship sent there for myself who have serv'd the Crown faithfully 24 Years, in Commission 12, There being no Officer in England who knows the Coast or place but My Self and I shall ever pray for your Lordships who am
Your Lords'
Most humble Obedient Servant
B. Young

Extract of a Representation from the Board of Trade to their Excellencys the Lords Justices, dated June 5th 1719

In Obedience to your Excellency's Commands signify'd to Us by M Delefaye in his Letter of the 28th of May last, We have considered the Memorial of Mons. Joannis Heriberry[[?]], relating to the Seizure made of his and other French Effects at Canceau by Captain Smart Comander of His Maj's Ship the Squirrel on the 18th day of Septr  1718 and have compar'd the same with the Accounts which We have receivd of this matter from Colonel Shute His Majestys Governor of the Massachusets Bay. Whereupon We beg leave to represent to your Excellencys

That Colonel Shute being informed, the Subject of the French King --from Cape Breton (now calld L'Isle Royal) had incroached upon His Majesty's Territorys in Nova Scotia, by taking possession of Canceau, and building Hutts in order to carry on a fishery there, in derogation of

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [4], 1717-1722
transcription:
512.

of the Right of the Crown of Great Britain. He did by the advice of His Majesty's C[[?]] dispatch Capt. Smart with Orders first, to take a View of what the French were doing[[?]] at Canceau, and thence to proceed to Cape Breton, and require the French Govr there to[[?]] recall them from thence. But in case of Refusal the said Smart was to seize a[[?]] their Effects & dislodge them by force, as b[[?]] a Copy of his Instructions hereunto ann[[?]] may now fully appear:

In pursuace of these Instructions Capt Smart saild from New England the 2[[?]] day of Augt 1618 for Canceau and from the[[?]] to Cape Breton, where having applyd w[[?]] out effect to the French Govt to recall Hi[[?]] most [[?]an Majestys Subjects from Canceau on the 14th day of Septr he returnd thither seizd upon several of their Effects, demo[[?]] their Hutts & repelld the French by force from thence as may appear by Captain Southacks journal who was joind with said Capt Smart in Comission to expostu[[?]] with the Govr of Cape Breton upon this Occasion, which Journal is likewise Here[[?]] annexd for your Excellency's further Information.

Thus

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [4], 1717-1722
transcription:
513.

Thus your Excellencys may perceive that Capt Smart's proceedings in this Affair were by Order of the Govr and Council of the Massachusets Bay, who We presume believed it was their Duty to assert, in this manner His Majesty's Right to the Lands or Islands where the Seizure was made; And altho a gentler method might possibly have been more advisable at so critical a Juncture, yet we cannot help thinking, that Col Shute of His Majesty's Council of the Massachusets Bay, have express'd upon this Occasion a very laudable Zeal for His Majesty's Service.

For upon the best Light We have hitherto been able to get into this matter, it would seem the French had no manner of reason to set up a Title to the Lands or Islands where the Seizure was made, or even to fish on that Coast. However if your Excellencys should be disposd in favour of the Memorialist and to cultivate a good Understanding between the two Nations to give your Orders to the Govr of the Massachusets Bay and Capt Smart Comander of His Majestys Ship the Squirrel to return the Vessels and Effects seizd by the latter at Canceau, We have nothing to object to 
it

Sir

I did not imagine I should have any Occasion of troubling you from hence, but being contrary to Expectation detained here 5 1/2 Weeks, judged  it necefiary that  their Lord be acquainted therewith to prevent any blame on me; near a Month has been spent in victualing & fitting the Kings Ship intending for the West Indies after setting me on Shore, & for the remaining time we have had contrary Winds & bad weather.

This Lofs of time has brought on the Winter, that by the time I get there all Communication will be shut up with Indians & the French till the Spring, so that their Lord ps: may not be surprised if they have not so early an Account of my Proceedings as they might expect. 

I have made the best Use of my time here by making known his Majesty's Resolution of taking the Country of Nova Scotia under his immediate Care & Protection and

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [4], 1717-1722
transcription:
520
and the Encouragement to be given toward the setling thereof, which I have reason to believe will bring many People from hence. Upon this Occasion I make one Observation viz: that upon perusing my Instructions I find it prohibited to make any Grants before a general Survey be made of hte Country, which tis[?] possible may take up more time than was thought, & by that means not only retard but in some measure obstruct the intended Settlement if People cannot be fit to to work for their livelyhood immediately upon their coming there therefore would humbly offer to their Lord:ps Consideration how to prevent that seeming ill Consequence; In the mean time I shall strictly pursue my Instructions.

I likewise desire their Lord:ps may be acquainted that I have spoke with some Fishermen lately come from Canso[?] who inform me that the French have been fishing there again this Summer, & made some thousands of Quirbals, which they carryed off under a Guard of Soldiers upon an Alarm of the Man of

You'll be pleased to communicate thus much to their Lordps & that I shall do my self the Honour of acquainting them from time to time of my Proceedings and the state of Affairs in that Country which is all that offers from

humble Servant
R Philips
Boston New England

To the Right Honourable the Lords of Trade and Plantations.
In humble obedience to your Lordships Commands to give our best account of the Scituation of the Isles of Canso, and other Circumstances relating to them, and in whose property and Dominion, according to the Treaty of the Crowns of Great Britain and France, which your Lordships have given us in three Languages.
After deliberate perusall and consideration, we say and are of the opinion, That the outmost Islands, which are a body of Rocks, and almost contiguous, give name to Cape Canso; being as we verily believe, six or seven Leagues distant Southwest from Saint Peters, an Harbour and Settlement on Cape Poritton; near the mouth of the Gulf of Canso; which Islands of Petit or Cape Canso are many, and only Little Gutts, seperate one from the other, as also as small a Gutt or Passage, separates these Islands, from the main Land; and without the least shadow to the Contrary, are absolutely and intirely given up, to be the property of Great Britain, as they are far distant from Cape Britten and more especially from the mouth or Gulf of St Lawrance, and even from the Gutt of Canso: which parts the main from the Island of Britton; so that we are humbly of opinion what is incerted in the small French map, is done with partiallity, purely to favour the last years French Fishery at Cape Canso: and is only the opinion of one man, formerly an Inhabitant of Annapolis, and removed thence and fished at Cape Canso, for the conveniency of Catching and Curing his Fish with most profit and advantages; which man took the Oath of Allegence to the Crown of Great Britain, as did two of the other four there settled, so that their allegation is intirely void; that being sett[[?]] with French men makes it belong to the Crown of France.

529.
Boston New England January the 13th-1718 2
Journal of Remarkable Transactions during the said voyage I have made by Order of His Excellency - Samual Shute Esqr. and Honble. His Majestyes Council in his Majestyes Ship Squrril Captain Thomas Smartt Comander.
We sailed from Nantuckett 26th day of August 1710, and arrived the 6th day of September at Canso Harbour in the Territories and Dominions of Nova Scotia Where we found a French Ship with a French White Flagg at the head of his Main Mast a Brigantine and Sloop with White Ensign Jack and Pendant, Each of them and about Thirty French Shallops afishing 7th Instant came into this Harbour from Louice Bourg, a place on Island of Breton, French Sloop with her white Ensign Leading with French Merchandize, to trade here; but Captain Smartt received a great many affronts here from the French but did not think it proper while his return from Louice Bourg to make any answer to them The 10th day of September We Sailed from Cansco Harbour and at 6 afternoon we got to Louis Bourg, being Twenty Three Leagues from Cansco, At 9 at Night St. Ovide De Brovillian the Governour of Island Breton sent the Captain of the Port to Captain Smartt to know his Business his answer was he would waite on the Governour to Morrow Morning and if the Governour would give him 9 Guns he would Salute him with 9 Guns 11th Instant at 9 Morning Captain Smartt and I went on Shore, and had a Conferrence about the boundaries of Nova Scotia and also the next day with St. Ovide De Brovillian the Governour and [[?]]oral more with him, then he was made Sensible that the French
have

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [4], 1717-1722
transcription:
530.
have nothing to do with any of the Continent, nor the Islands of Cansco Captain Smartt at the same time demanded in the King of Great Britain's Name that he would give to the French that were there at Cansco, to retire to the [[?]] Territories, and Offered to Allow him any reasonable [[?]] for them to withdraw themselves and Effects but he refused. then Captain Smartt made an open Protestation against the proceedings of the French at Cansco, And Assured the Governour that it would be resented by the English Government and that Measures would be taken accordingly. The 13th of September We Sailed from Louis Bourg, 14th [[?]] we Arrived at Cansco, where the French ship had out [[?]] white flagg and the other French vessells as before [[?]] French Colours out. The 10th September Captain Smartt [[?]] Seizuers of the French Ship Brigantine and Sloop and [[?]] Fishe[[?]] the French on the shoar belonging to the ship other French Inhabitants and some other goods which Sent some of them goods ashoar against my desire.
25th of September Captain Smart Delivered the French ship to the French Captain again by reason he had no[[?]] to Man her to bring her for Boston In New England [[?]] brought the Brigantine and Sloop away with him, we came to Saile Several Vessells more in Company.
4th day of October We Arrived at Boston 1718.
Cyprian Stuthack

531.
To his Excellency Samuel Shute Esqr Captain General and Governour in Chief and the Honble Council of his Majestye's Province of the Massachusetts Bay in New England - 
The Memorial of Cyprian Southack - 
Humbly Sheweth - 
That on the Eleventh day of April in the year 1713 within the time of the Suspension of Arms between the Two Crowns of Great Britain and France Your Memorialist being then in the service of this Government on a Message to Accquaint all Privateers on the Coast of Cape Sables with the Cessation of which he did Accordingly therebeing then Three French Privateers at Port Le Tour yet Notwithstanding the Notice given them by Publick Proclamations of the Suspension of Arms they from your Memorialist a Fishing Sloop and drove home Another which he Carried with him Whereby your Memorialist was a Looser the sum of Two hundred pounds. - 
That on the Eleventh day of July 1715 Your Memorialist under Governor Duddlley's Warrant being ashoar at Cape Rosaway on the Coast of Nova Scotia - with Three fishing Vessels Vizt Two Sloops and a Scooner where of he was the Sole owner at which place he landed all his Stores and built Two houses ashoar for the Carrying on his Fishery, and after your Memorialist had been
Some

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [4], 1717-1722
transcription:
some time at Port Rosaway aforesaid and had made Considerable Advances in his Fishery one Tauranguer a French man and Jo: Muse part Indian who dwelt at Port Le Tore aforesaid came to your Memorialist and Told him they would head One hundred Indians to Destroy all English Fishery on that Coast the said Taranguer and Muse having some time before Sworne Allegieance to the Crown of Great Britain at Anapolis Royall.
That Monsieur Costable Governour of Cape Breton made a present of Two hundred pounds to the Indians to take from your Memorialist what he had and then to kill him Whereof your Memorialist had private Intelligence by some of the Indians that they designed Speedily to put in Execution their barbarous Intention. title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
V9. 480.
To the Right Hon:ble the Lords Commissioners for Trade & Plantations

The humble Representation of Peter Capon
Sheweth
                          The pursuant to Your Lordships Commands, he humbly takes leave to represent his Observations on the State of the Province of Nova Scotia as follows.
   Annapolis Royal the chief place in Nova Scotia is situated on a pleasant River, navigable seven Leagues above the Garrison and the Land about very fruitfull, producing excellent Corn, which by the long Wars they have been hindred from fully cultivating, but a few years Peace will make both Corn and Cattel very plentifull, and there wants only more Inhabitants to make it a flourishing Colony.
    Up the Bay of Fundy to the North East of Annapolis, is a District called Minos, very fruitfull in Corn & Cattle, and the best inhabited of any Part of the Bay, next to this is another Tract called Chiginectoo, wch is also well inhabited, & has Mines of Sea Cole as good as any in Great Britain appearing out of the Ground, and so near the Rivers, as to be digged and loaded on Board with little trouble, as are also plenty of good Grindstones.
   Near this is a large Tract of marshy Land, made by the confluences of Several Rivers called Tintamare, where are but four Familys settled, tho' capable of subsisting great Numbers.
   The upper part of the Bay is called Caubegit, where are Several Families who have plenty of Cattle, which they drive thro' the Woods in five Days time to a Place call'd Hartigaunich, a great Place of Rendevous for the Indians, where the French have a Missionary who has a Chappel. At this place are Boats always ready by which they transport their Cattle to Cape Breton. From this on the North Side of the Bay, is a great Tract of Land uninhabited, as far as to a large River called the River of St Johns, where is but one french Family tho' many Indies here are plenty of large Masts, out of which the late french King, chiefly supply'd his Navy, as also great quantities of good Salmon. The Indians go in their Canoes up this River towards Canada, to sell their Peltry to buy European Goods. The next place of note to this is Pasmaquady (near the Mouth of the Bay) a place very convenient for Saw Mills, and from whence Planck might be furnish'd both good and Cheap. Here is but one french Family tho' many Indians.
    From Pasmaquady to Penobscot towards New England is a large Coast with many good Harbours, tho' uninhabited. At Penobscot (where are but two French Familys) are many fruitfull Islands & a great Settlement of Indians who have a Fort, and are the most industrious of any on that Coast.
   The Chief Harbours or places of Trade & fishing on the Coast, round from Annapolis to Cape Breton, are first Grand Passages, where is an Island very fitt for a Settlement. The next is the Cape and Bay of St. Maries, from thence to Cape Torcheu, and so to Poumecou and round by Cape Sables along the Coast to Port
                                                                             Rasway

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
Rasway. All this Coast is full of good Harbours and well stock'd with fish, both spring and fall. At Port Rasway are excellent Beaches for curing of fish and abundance of Apple Trees growing tho' the Inhabitants are all driven off.
  Another place of Note, nearer to Cape Breton, is La Have, where the french had a Garrison tho' now there remains but Six Families. From thence the Coast extends to Merlegesh, another good fishing Place, and So to Chibouctou, where the French designed to have built a Fort, and settled for their chief place of Trade.
   From Chibouctou along the Coast about 80 Leagues to the North East (in which Distance are many good Harbours & fishing Places tho' uninhabited except by strolling Indians) lyes little Canceau which is but four Leagues from Petit de Gra, a place where the French have a Settlement & designe to build a Fortification. This Petit de Gra is on an Island called Ladys Island, on which the French have another Settlement and is separated from Cape Breton by s Gut, which Ships of 40 Tons may sail thro at Low Water.
       The Inhabitants of Nova Scotia are all French, (except all the Garrison of Annapolis & the Indians and pretty numerous about the Bay of Fundy, especially at Annapolis Minos, to Chiginectoo; They were also numerous from that Bay along the Coast to little Canceau, but are mostly driven off by the late and former War. They have great plenty of Corn and Cattle, and abound with Fish, and the Land with all Sorts of Masts, & other Timber. The Inhabitants make Tarr for their own use; and account it better than that which is produced in other Parts of America, being not Subject to any burning quality, tho' they never prepare any Trees for that purpose. The Soil is generally very good and great Tracts of it proper for hemp, of which there is Some growing Wild.
        It would be of great Advantage both to this Kingdom & y Plantations if this Colony were better settled than it is at present.
1st  By reason of its Situation, it being near the french settlements of Cape Breton & Canada, that if there were more Fortifcations built, they would not only be a great Protection to the Fishery & Trade of Nova Scotia, but would be a Curb to the french Privateers from Cape Breton, in case of a Rupture, and very convenient for anoying the French in their Trade, both there, and up the River Canada.
2d  A good Settlement of English Inhabitants would bring the Indians to our Interest, by bring their Peltry & Furs and furnishing them with European Goods near their own Settlements, which they now fetch from Cape Breton and Quebec. This would prove a very beneficial Trade to Great Britain, by taking of great quantitys of the Woollen Manufactures, and yielding very advantageous Return for the same.
3d The Winds during the Summer Season blow, on that Coast, generally, South West, which is against the New England Ships in their Return home, and for want of Protection in Nova Scotia are discouraged from building
Stages there and therefore carry all their Fish home to cure; which by reason of the Distance, and the contrary Winds is oft spoil'd before it comes to the Stage, to the great loss of the Fishermen, besides two thirds of their time is spent in going & coming, which might be employ'd in the Fishery.

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
In order to advance the Settlement it's humbly proposed
1st  That when ever it may be thought for his Majesty's Service, that a Reform be made of the Troops in Great Britain, those now at Annapolis, may be reliev'd, and supply'd with a double Number from hence; and if his Majesty Shall not think fit to maintain so large a Garrison, then at the end of    Months after their arrival to discharge so many of the Soldiers, as Shall desire it, or Shall appear the least fit for Service, leaving only Such a Number, as His Majesty appoint to secure the Fortifications. These Soldiers so disbanded, will by seeing the fruitfulness of the Country be encouraged to settle there, and help to plant the Colony.
2. To Send a Governour thither with Instructions to grant a certain number of Acres of Land in fee to every Soldier or other Person who Shall go or stay to settle there; as is usual in other Plantations, with a Proviso in Such Grant, for cultivating in a certain time, Such a proportion there of as Shall be thought reasonable; or else Such Grant to be void, and the Land to revert to the Crown, in order to be regranted to Such Person as will improve it.
3d  In regard the Province at present is So little improv'd, that all necessarys for the poor Soldiers are very scarce & dear, and the Deducting their provisions out of their pay makes them inexpressibly miserable. It's humbly proposed that they be allow'd their Provisions Gratis as is done in Several other Garrisons both in Europe & America. This would induce others to enter cheerfully into that Service, and instead of their being the Contempt of the Inhabitants, they would marry there, and as they become Invalids, would Save Chelsea Hospital the Charge of Maintaining them, by helping to raise an English Colony in Nova Scotia.
               The following Places are humbly recommended as proper to be fortif'd, in order to secure the Trade & Fishery, incourage Settlements, & protect the Inhabitants in the Manufactures of Naval Stores.
1.  Port Rasway for it's convenient Situation, good Beaches, & the great Resort of fishing Vessels to it, and also it's fruitfull Soil and having been an old Settlement, and by Consequence the easier resettled.
2. Chibouctou, as lying in the Center of the Coast from Annapolis to Canceau, and being So contiguous to Minos that the Inhabitants passing in Canoes up a River [[illegible line, page folded]] and from thence to Annapolis in Three morem so that the two Garrisons, tho' a great Distance by Sea, would be able to help each other in Ten Days time by Land.
3.. Little Canceau, where is a good Fishery and fine Beaches, for curing the Fish catch'd along that Part of the Coast, about Isles Sables, to the Banks adjacent. For want of a Fortification at this Place, the neighboring Fishery, which is exceeding good, will naturally fall into the hands of the French, they having Protection at Cape Breton, but the English none thereabouts, and especially in Case of a Rupture, for then it would be so 
                                                                                  neglected

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
481. 482.

neglected by the English, that the French would again gett footing on the Continent with Ease, it being So near their own Settlements and Fortifications.
     But in case it not be thought [[free?]] to build So many Forts at once then Chignectou is recomended for the first as being a Place that will be most easily settled, and the Garrison best assisted with fresh Provisions to preserve their health from the Neighboring Settlement of Minos.

            I am now to answer your Letter of 10th Inst: N.S., as well as I can at present, but as the Lords Justices have referr'd  to the Board what you writ to Mes: Delasaye about the French Fishing at Canço, I doubt not but that they will report upon it with more Exactness than I am able to do, if they can get any further Information than what they've had already. However in the mean time I would not lose this Opportunity of giving you the best Information I am able.

   Capt. Smart, who wou'd have been of Service upon this Occasion, is not yet arriv'd from New England.

Cape Canço is the Eastermost Cape of the Main Land of Nova Scotia before one comes in to the [[Gut?]] of Canço & forms a Bay called Canço Bay, or Richilabucktoo, And that the French have fish'd there upon that Continent will appear to you from the inclos'd

                                                                   Consequence

From the Grand Prez, at Minas.
                                                                   May 14, 1720

May it please Your Excellency

   I doe my Self the Honour to acquaint you that Your Excellencys Proclamations sent [[to Blin?]] was published here by Father Felix, the day before my arrival, and this Letter comes to your hand by the Sieur Alexander Bourg, one of the Deputys they have Chosen, the people in general here seem to be much concerned, loath to leave their Habitations and Estates their Ancesters left them, and afraid to stay and Possess them under the Nomination of English to have their Throats cutt by the Indians most of them notwithstanding flatter themselves with hopes that your Excellency will please to extend your Pitty, and Compassion to them, their Wives and little Ones, and not force them away they know not where, because they dare not take the Oath of Allegiance, the doing of which would expose them to the Insults of the Indians, but they say the Government cannot charge them with disobedience since they took the Oath to her Majesty Queen Anne, and that they are ready, and will promise to be Loyall, and faithful to King George and Obedient to the Government if that may suffice till things are better regulated with the Indians, they say also they were in hopes to reap some benefit from her Majestys most gracious Letter in their favour whereby they had

                                                                                 leave

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
418. 

leave to sell their moveable, and imoveables if they went off, which they are forced to doe by the Proclamation several of them have desired me to Represent these their Greviences to your consideration professing themselves a poor Ignorant People having One amongst them acquainted with the Affairs of the World, and that what they doe is not in [[complaint?]] of his Majesty, or the Government, but to preserve their Lives

The Father Justinien staid a few days here, and went to Checunectook in order to goe to Cape Breton; In sd discourse I had with Father Felix yesterday he excused himself that he could not waite on the General at the time, there was a Sick Person, of whom he must receive confession, and that part of his Parrish at Pigigit had not fait leurs Pasque, but that the Father Justinien would bring an Officer of Distinction with him from Cape Breton, who would assemble all the Inhabitants here and goe with them and he would take that opportunity to waite on the General with them he praised the constancy of the Inhabitants who (as he said) declared when they were assembled they would doe no otherwise than what they did with the Two French Officers were here in General Nicholson's time that he and they would all goe away together [[?]] the Island St. Johns under the French Kings Domain. he found great fault with the Proclamation that [[?word]] Publick was not inserted to
Exercise of Religion that by that was meant only in their owne Houses, as in England and Ireland, and the 

                                                                                 clause

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722

The Indians also are very buisy on this occasion going from place to place, to inform one another they have been Robed a Challop at Cobagil of thirty or Forty Pounds worth of Goods, that four French's Men had bought of Mr. Blin, and carried there to Trades: I hear it whispered among the French that all the Indians farr, and near, are expected here in a Months time, and by the hints they gave you may have an Army of French this Sumer at Annapolis Royall, whether in an hostile manner or no I know not: I met with the chief of the Indians of Chenenectook here with several others his followers, to whom I delivered the Message your Excellency was pleased to charge me with; he seemed well pleased, but said the English were very dilatory in settling affairs with them, but they were ready to come to a good agreement with the English when you pleased to appoint them to come.

I begg your Excellency Pardon for troubling you with this long Letter, but think it my duty, since you have been pleased to Honour me to sitt with your Excellency at his Majestys Councill Board, and must say with Submission that it is my humble Opinion, it would be for His Majesty's Service, and the more speedy settlement of this Collony if the French Inhabitants might be permitted to stay on such conditions, as Your Excellency

transcription:
Par son Excellence Richard Philipps Escuyer Capitaine General et Gouverneur en Chef de la Province de sa Majeste La Nouvelle Escosse ou Accadie.

Nonobstant les faveurs ou Intentions de bonté que Sa Sacrée Majesté Le Roy de la Grande Bretagne etc. a bien voulu M'ordonner de Communiquer aux Habitants François demeurant dans cette Sienne Province de La Nouvelle Escosse et Accadie Ce que de mon Cote J'ay Publié dans un Proclamation portant [[faite?]] du 19e Jour d'Avril 1720 V.S. et J'ay depuis mis en resage touts les moyens possibles que J'ay vu pouvoir estre particuliorient utiles au Bien et a l'Interest des dits Habitants, auquelles Marques de Bonté que leur ont Ctte' Montrées ils ont Jusques icy repondre avec [[Ingratitude?]] Sur tout pour leur etc. etc. dernier Mespris et désobeissance a ce que J'envois requis deux, qui n'estoit que pour leur Bien present et avenir, Comme euisse pour l'entreprise que J'apprens que les Habitants de cette Riviere ont formée de Couper une Communication au travers des Bois Jusque aux Memes, et qui ont envoyé demander aux Habitants de ce dernier endroit de les assister en coupent leur part, [[Soins?]] M'en demander permission ou Seulement M'en donner la connoissance le quel procèdé temeroire et Inconsideré me donne Juste raison de croire qu'ils ont des Mechants dessigns Sur pied, ou de faire Venir pour La ditte Communication un Nombre de Gens pour Molester cette
Garrison de la Majesté, ou bien d'emporter ou emmener leurs offetset leur betoiel d'icy, et de former une Assemblée generale aux Memes ou a Chignecgto, pour le Maintenir un [[dessy?]] de Sa Majesté et du Gouvernement.
    C'est pourquoy Je donne Ordre positivement et Je Commande ponctuellement ce toutes Sortes de Personnes de se desister tout aussy [[?]] d'une belle entreprise, et S'ils estoient offez obstinez pour desobeir a ces Ordres cy, Je Serai Obligé de regarder ce procedé comme un Acte de Defiance a l'autorité du Roy, et de prendre les Moyens que Je croirai les plus propres a conserver ce gouvernement et cette Province de Soi Majesté, et J'ordonne de plus  qu'aucune Personne ne quitte Son Habitation en Cochette et Sans en avoir ma Permission. Donné a Annapolis Royalle le 18e May 1720.
