To His Excellency Lords. Shute Esq Cap: General and Gov.r in Chief in and Over His Majesty's Province of the Massachusets ets.Bay etc. and Vice Admiral of the Same & to the Honble: His Majesty's Council & Representatives in Gen: Court Assembled this 9 June 1718.

                     The Meml: of James Pits, Olivr: Noyes In Marshall etc. in behalf of themselves & partners concerned in the Fishery.

That Cape Canso in the Territory of Le Accadie, or Nova Scotia, being a Harbour Accommodated for the making or curing Fish, having invited Your Mem. lists with other of His Majesty's Subjects to fit out and furnish a considerable number of Fishing Vessels with their Stores for the Summers Voyage etc. to Erect houses & Stages, and to make all necessary Provisions for the curing their Fish, in the said Harbor of Canso, on which very considerable Sums are already Expended, and more daily advancing; That the Said Harbour and Shoar with the Fort then Fort Lewis was taken from the French by Cap: Cyprian Southack in the Year 1690, and possession taken by him for the Crown of Great Britain in the Year 1714 and never possessed by the French Since the Caption until now.  That the Said Harbour & Shoar were Yielded up by His Most Christian Majesty to the Crown of Great Britain in the Treaty of Utrecht as by the 12, 13 & 14 Articles of the Said Treaty will plainly Appear.

That Lieut Young in His Majesty's Ship Rose called in at the Said Harbour of Canso in the Year 1716, and finding about 30 French Shallops a fishing there he Ordered them away & received for answer that they acknowledged it to be within the English Boundaries, and that they would be gone etc.

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
403.

 Instructions given to Cap: Tho: Smart Commander of His Majesty's Shop Squirrel for his Conduct in his designed Negotiation at Cap Cançeo and Cape Breton.

Whereas Complaints have been made to me by his Majesty's good Subjects concerning ye Fishery at Cape Cançeo of the encroachments of ye French upon them by Fishing on the English ground and Setting up Huts and other Buildings & Curing their Fish on that Shoar, and their Ships Loading in the English Harbour, together with their Menaces to dispossess the English of that Place, and their Exciting the Indian Savages to insult them and disturb them in the Enjoym:t of those Privileges to which as Englishmen they are Entitled; I have therefore thought fit by the advice and at the desire of his Majesty's Council of this Province, to order you in his Majesty's Ship Squirrel under your Command to repair to Cape Cançeo  & inform yourself particularly of the grounds of those Complaints & if you find those Accounts to be true, and that the French have given disturbance to the English and encroached upon his Majesty's Territories, as is represented : You are first to go over to Cape Breton, and after delivery of my Letter to the Gov.r of that place, you are to enquire of him whether those proceedings of the French have been of his countenance & Approbation, which if he disowns you are to give immediate Orders. that they withdraw themselves their Ships and Boats from Cape Cançeo and the Coast thereabouts & that there be no further cause of Complaint of the like injuries for the future. If the Gov.r owns his Approbation of the Actions of the French as before Expressed, you are to make a plain & open protestation of the Injustice thereof &

                                                                                    the

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
404. 

the Breach thereby made of the Treaty of Peace, concluded at Utrecht as well as an infringement of the Rights of the English to the Said Land by much older claim. You are thereupon to Shew to the Gov:r the Treaty of Peace made at Utrecht and urge from the 12th and 13th Articles thereof of the indisputable Title of the English to the Sd Country & Coast & in the Kings Name to demand that Justice be Speedily done to the English in that Affair & Assure ye Gov.r that the disturbances given to their Enjoyment of that place if Supported & Vindicated will be resented by the English Governm:t as a plain notorious Violation of the Treaty of Peace between the two Nations & measures will be taken by these accordingly. After which you are to allow the Said Gov:r a reasonable time to bring off the People & their Effects from Cape Cançeo ; And if [[?]]no compliance be made to your demands you are to Seize upon what Fish & other Effects you find within the English Limits & bring it off with you, & to demolish whatsoever Buildings the French have Set up there; and compel the French People to quit the Said place, except Such of the Said Nation as are friendly to the English, and have their leave to reside among them.  You are by all means to endeavor the Effecting your business without bloodshed, & not proceed So far unless urged to it by plain and evident necessity. I have order'd Captain Cyps. Southack to accompany you in this voyage he has the Vote of the Council to assist you in your Negotiation, he has a perfect knowledge of the Boundaries of those Countries & carries with him a good Draught thereof, & has had long Experience of the Customs and Manners of the French inhabitants there.  You are therefore to do nothing of Moment[[?]] without his Assistance.

                                                                   Signed

 To Cap: Thomas Smart                      Sam:l Shute
 Command:r of His Majesty's
Ship Squirrel.

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
1 copy         405.

Copy of a Letter from his Excellency Sam:l Shute Esq. Gov:r of New England to the Gov:r of Cape Breton by Capt. Tho: Smart

   I have had Complaints made to me by several of his Majesty's good Subjects of this Province who have undertook the Fishing Business at Cape Canso of the Encroachments of the French particularly those under your Government on the Territories of the King of Great Britain, my Master. I would hope that such Irregularities can have no Countenance from You, & therefore I have thought it most condusive to that good Understanding w:ch ought to be kept up between the Subjects of the two Crowns to ask the proper Redress from You before I proceed to other Methods of asserting & vindicating the Rights of the King of Great Britain reserv'd & secur'd to him by the Treaty of Utrecht; By Letters from several English Merchants now residing at Cape Canso I am inform'd that there is a great Number of the French already come over thither, that they have set up Stages & Houses on that Shoar & that there is a French Ship in that Harbour & more expected; I need not tell You that if these Proceedings are abetted & favour'd by the French Governm:t they will be accounted an open & notorious Infraction of the 12th & 13th Articles of the Treaty of Utrecht.

   In the 12th Article it is agreed that the British Subjects be possess'd of all Nova Scotia with its ancient Boundaries, and that the Subjects of the most Christian King shall be hereafter excluded from all kind of Fishing in the Seas Bays & other Places on the Coast of Nova Scotia that is to say of those which lye towards the East within 30 Leagues of the Isle of Sables inclusively, & thence the whole Continent of Nova Scotia is included;

  In the 13th Article its agreed that Island called Cape Breton as also all other Islands in the Mouth of the River of St Lawrence & in the Gulph of that Name shall hereafter
                                                                              belong

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
406.

belong of Right to the French; so that no other Lands but the Islands being given to the French they can upon no Colour or Pretence of Justice settle themselves upon Canso, which is the Continent of Nova Scotia & does of Right belong to the King of Great Britain as much as any other Part of his Majesty's Dominions; I have therefore sent Capt. Tho. Smart in his Ma'tys Ship Squirrel to demand in the King's Name that Orders be immediately given to the French that are gone over to Cape Canso to Fish on that Shoar & make their Fish on the Land there to withdraw & return to the French Territories, & that the French Ships or Vessels now riding in the English Harbours be order'd to depart & that His Majesty's good Subjects have no further Molestation on the Use of those Privileges which they claim by the ancient Rights of the Kings of Great Britain, & by the said Treaty of Utrecht by which the same is strengthen'd & confirm'd.  I am etc;

                                                                  Saml Shute

  Copy of the Answer to the foregoing Letter.

V:
                                         Mr. Tho: Smart Cap:t of the Vessel of the King of Great Britiain who arriv'd in this Port the 21st [[?]] has deliver'd me the Letter which You did me the Honour to write me, in which You advise me You has receiv'd some Complaints from some of Your Subjects settled at the Islands and Harbour of Canso by means of those of the King of France that are there a fishing who have made me the said Complaints; & took the Opportunity of going there the beginning of June where after I had given such Orders as I thought necessary for the Tranquility of the two Nations  I wrote about it to Mr. Philipps thinking he was arriv'd at his Government & advised him what I thought proper on the Posture of the
                                                                                  present

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
407.

present Affairs; This day We have had a serious Conference on this Subject with Mr. Smart & Capt. Cyprian Southack where we expos'd our Rights on one Part & t'other conformable to the Treaty of Peace made at Utrecht. The Difference which We found in the 12th Article between that of which he is the Bearer & that which I have, occasion'd Us to give reciprocally Copies of the 12 & 13th Articles w:ch We have each of Us sign'd for himself conformable to the Originals. You will remark by the 12th of yours that the Points of Compass are not equal, & moreover there is no mention made of the 30 Leagues near the Coasts of Nova Scotia as it is in mine which on this Occasion causes a very great Error, so that tis impossible to come to any Agreement at present where the ancient Limits might be or ought to be, for according to your Rhombe of the wind You bear much on the Royal Island according to Ours We border about the River of St. Mary:

      I don't think it convenient for private Subjects who ought to be no more than Interpreters of the Orders of the Kings their Masters to decide Points so nice & where Difficulties may be found which can't be remov'd, but by the Decision of the two Crowns, nevertheless I have offer'd Mr. Smart to withdraw after the Fishery is over to other Places of the Royal Island, all the French Inhabitants that are at Canso & thereabouts, provided that he would likewise evacuate the English Inhabitants that are there until We had a perfect Decision from Our Courts: I know Sr. how Strict the Knots are which unite Our two Crowns & I should be very sorry to do any thing that might give any Occasion to break them. I am persuaded that You are of the same Opinion; I am going to inform the Council of what We have done & reckon I shall have positive News next Spring of what has been regulated thereon.  I shall not fail of advising You of the Orders I shall receive from the King my Master on this Affair, hoping You'll impart to me what You shall have.  I am etc.

LouisBourg the Royal Island    Sr Ovide de Brouillon
23d Septem: 1717

mise copy                                409.

Boston New England  Oct.r 4th 1718

A Journal of Remarkable Transactions during the Voyage I have made by Order of His Excellency Samuel Sharpe Esq:r, and the Hon:ble his Majesty's Council in his Majesty's Ship Squirrel Capt. Thomas Smart Commander.

We sail'd from Nantasket 26th Day of August 1718 arriv'd the 6th Day of Sep.r at Canço Harbour on the Territories & Dominions of Nova Scotia, where we found a French Ship with a French White flag at the Head of his Main Mast, a Brigantine & a Sloop with White Enseigns, Jack & Pendant, each of them & about thirty French Shallops a fishing; 7 Inst. came into this Harbour from Louisbourg, a place on Island of Breton French Sloop with her White Ensign lading with Merchansdize to trade here, but Cap:t Smart receiv'd a great many affronts here from the French, but did not think it proper until his Return, from Louisbourg to make any Answer to them.  This 10th Day of Sept'r we sail'd from Canço Harbour & at 6 Afternoon we got to Louisbourg being twenty three Leagues from Canço, at 9 at Night Sr. Ovide De Brouillian the Gov.r of Sd Island Breton sent the Capt. of ye Port to Cap:t Smart to know his Business, his Answer was he wou'd wait on the Gov:r tomorrow Morning. And if the Gov:r wou'd give

                                                               him,

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
him 9 Guns, he wou'd salute him with nine Guns. The 11th Inst. at 9 in the Morning Capt. Smart & I went on Shore & had a Conference about the Boundaries of Nova Scotia, and also the next day with Sr. Ovide De Brouillian the Gov.r & several more with him, who was made Sensible that the French have nothing to do with any part of the Continent nor the Islands of Canço. Cap't Smart at the same time demanded in the King of Great Britains name that he wou'd give Orders to the French that [[?]]then at Canço to retire to the French Territories & offer'd to allow him any reasonable time [[?]] them to withdraw themselves & Effects but he refused, then Capt. Smart made an open Protestation against the Proceedings of the French at Canço, assured the Governor it would be resented by the English Governor & that Measures wou'd be taken accordingly.

The 13t of Sept we Sail'd from Louisbourg

The 14th Inst. we arriv'd at Canço where the French Ship had out her White flag the other French Vessels as beforementioned French Colours out.

The 18t of September Capt. Smart [[?]] Seizures of the French Ship Brigantine [[?]] Sloop & some fish of the French on the [[?]] belonging to their Ships and other French Inhabitants & some other Goods, of which he sent some of them a Shoar again by [[?]] Desire.  The 25 of Septem. Capt. Smart deliver'd the French Ship to the French Captain again and by Reason he had not Men to [[?]] her to bring her to Boston in New England.

My Lords

       To the 1st, I am of Opinion that the Methods us'd, do not make the 2d. Agreement null & void.

        For I observe that the 2d Agreement is not a new Convention but it founded upon the first Capitulation mutually agreed to 4th April 106 for the v l IX Articles provided.

v    "Que tous les Negres me seront remis [[Sec'd?]]

IX  "Que me sera remis quatre Hostages."

Now the Negros being to be deliver'd up; as p. Art: v; And it appearing by the Paper [[underlined]] We whose names etc.[[end of underline]] 6th April 1706, that
6023 Negros were then on the Island; And
                                                                    D'Iberville

   To the 2d I am of Opinion, that the Inhabitants are not acquitted from all manner of Obligations to perform their part.

      For they enjoy the Cession of the Island by Virtue of the paper; [[underlined]]Les presentes Lettres[[end of underline]]dated 19th April 1706, [[?]] the Damages of Waste committed after ye [[Date?]] thereof & the carrying off some Negros--cannot stand in Discharge of all manner of Obligations to perform their parts, the Cession of the Island being a valuable Consideration for the Agreement , but the Damages & taking of Negros subsequent to the Date thereof, may be computed to set off in part of Satisfaction of such these Obligations.

Extract of a Representation of the Board of Trade to the Lord Justices Octo : 4th 1700 relating to the Defence of New York, Sets Forth;

That the Province of New York being the most advanced Frontier of His Majesty's Plantations in those parts, the Defence and preservation thereof is of the utmost Importance to the Security of all the rest; not only with respect to the French of Canada, but against any insurrection of the Scattered Nations of Indians, upon that Continent.

   That the Forts and Fortifications on that Frontier for want of timely repairs, in so ruinous a Condition that they will now Scarce bear the firing of a Gun upon them.

   That the Soldiers which were formerly four Companies of 100 Men each, being diminished by Death and Desertion to less than 200 in the whole, and afterwards reduced by a New Establishment to 50 Men in each Company; are in a miserable condition almost Naked and ready to Perish by reason of ye great Arrears that are due unto them

   That Our five Nations of Indians who in the begining of the late War consisted of 3500, are now reduced to about 1100; having Suffered 
                                                                                 great

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
362.

great loss during the War, and many of them having been clandestinely Murdered by the French Indians Since the Peace; by reason of which weakness, they are now inclined to Shelter themselves under that Protection, which appears to them to be the Strongest.

  That the Posture of the French at Canada is much different from Ours; they maintain in constant pay 1500 Men, and are at Work with great Dilligence in repairing all their Forts, of which they have 8 or 9 between Quebeck & Mountreal (within the Space of 60 Leagues) besides other Fortifications at a greater distance (as for instance one in the Donaganaks [[Odanak]]Country 700 Miles from Quebeck) by which means they endeavour to extend their Territories on the back of His Majesty's Dominious  & Seem to prepare for War.

    That the French by reason of the Small Forts lying near one another, encourage their own People to inhabit and make Settlements on their Borders; and by means of their remoter Forts, they drive a Trade, and keep up an Intrest with the Indians, that live at distance, and have greatly animated them in their War against Ours.

   The the French Emissaries, have Spread Malicious Reports to fill Our five Nations-- with Prejudices, as if His Majesty had given
                                                                                       Orders

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
363.

Orders to disarm and Extirpate them; And that my Lord Bellomont would use means to destroy them by Poison which Suggestions--together with the consideration of Our Weakness, and the Strength of the French, have made Our Indians very Wavering in their Friendship towards Us, So that their Defection to the French is to be apprehended; And if that Should be followed with the conjunction of all the other Indians in those parts, it would be of fatal consequences, to the English Intrest on that Continent.

 We beg leave to add to Your Excellencies That Mons' D'Iberville Com. of a French Man of War of 50 Guns in his return from Missisipi to France in July last, put into the Fort of N. York (tho much out of his Way) upon pretence to Wood and Water, but more probably with a Design to Sound that Channel & Harbour.

   Upon this general View of Affairs ye Earl of Bellomont proposes, 

   That the Fortifications of the Province of New York be repaired; and more particularly that those of Albany & Shenectady, on ye Frontiers towards Canada be rebuilt with Stone of ye Charge of which according to Col. Romer the Ingineer's computation, will amount to 8 or 9000 Pds., And that two new Forts be erected, one to the N. Eastward of Albany at the end of a Lake called Colaers or the Iroquois Lake, and another in ye Orondage [[Onandaga]] Country, which lies to the N. Westward and is the Centre of the Habitation of Our five Nations, and 

                                                                                           opp.

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
364.

                            opposite to ye French Fort at Cadaraqui, by which Our Indians are much annoy'd, & their Trade obstructed. The Expence of building which Fort in ye Onondage Country, Col. Romer computed at 10 or 1200  pounds.

   And in Order to the repairing or building of these Forts His Lords: desires that Spades, Shovels and other Necessary Utensils be Sent from hence.

   His Lordship intends also to propose ye building of Several other Forts not only in the Province of New York but elswhere, which he conceives will be absolutely necessary for the Security of all His Majesty's Plantations on that Continent, & therefore advises, that his Majesty may be pleased to write Circular Letters to the Gov:r and Assemblies of each respective Plantation, to excite them to contribute to the Charge, but promises to explain himself further upon that Subject, and to Send his reasonings there upon, by the next conveyance. 

    For the Garisoning the Forts above mention'd for the Encouragement of Our Indians to continue firm in their Dependance on the Crown of England and in Gen:l for the Defence of those Frontiers his Lord:p proposes that 1000 Soldiers are absolutely necessary; And for ye better removing of any obstruction that might arise from the Charge of this Establishm't: , he has made a Scheme (which will be laid before Your Excell:s in the Sequel of this Representation) whereby the Labour of these Soldiers in making Turpentine, Tar, Rozin and Pitch, may defray the Charge of their maintenance.

  His Lords:p offers that the Lt. Col.: may be made Lt. Gov:r of New Hampshire;  the Major Gov:r of Albany; with Such Additional Salaries as His Majesty may be pleased to allow; and that the Captains be of the King's Council, both in New York & New Hampshire. 

             His Lord:p  Offers, that Some Minister of the Church of England, be sent to live among Our Indians. to instruct them in Christianity, and to prevent their being practised upon by the French Priests and Jesuits.

           Having received a Letter from Boston in New England, dated the 2d of Sept. last, in which I have the following Paragraph,

Sir

   This Morning arriv'd at Boston from Canco on the Coast of Nova Scotia Mrs. Henshaw's Son in a Sloop, who brings the bad news of the French setting the Indians upon the English fishery there the 15th of Aug:st 1720 with French amongst them & seiz'd to the Value of ten thousand pounds Sterling in Fish & Merchandize, & carry'd it over to Cape Breton & killed three English Men; The English have taken several of the French that were in this Action & have sent them Prisoners to Governor Philips at Annapolis Royal.

Memorial,

                   To St. Ovide De Brovillian, Govr of Island Breton in North America, concerning Anciens Boundaries of Nova Scotia or Accadie, Sep: 11 1718.


        The whole Country of Nova Scotia as far Eastward as Cape St. Lawrence, was Seiz'd for the Crown of Great Britain about the Close of the 18th Century, by Sebastian Cabot, Grand Pilot to Henry 7th King of Great Britain, & by him sent to find out Such parts of North America; King James the 1st therefore knowing his Title to be good, did in 1621, make a Grant of this Country, to Sir Wm Alexander, afterwards Earl of Sterling, who Settled a Colony there, by the Name of Nova Scotia. Upon the Marriage of King Charles the first with the Lady Henrietta Maria, it was by Order of the King given up to the French in the Year 1627, in 1628, We got it again, and was given to Sir David Kirk, who was both Proprietor and Gov.r of the North Side of the River called Canada, and South side called Accadie; it fell again into the hands of Sir Wm Alexander, in the Years 1632 it was given away again to the French King, who Oblig'd himself to pay in Lieu of the Forts 9000 to Sir David Kirk which he never did.

Cromwell weighing the premises Sent Colonel Sedgwick in 1654, and retook it, And when he made Peace with France the following Year,

                                                                                    tho'

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [3], 1717-1722
transcription:
382.

   tho's their Ambassador made pressing [[Intreaties?]] for the restitution of it, yet he would not part with it, insisting that it was by ye Amical Inheritance of the Crown of England. And by right belonged to it; Whereupon Mons'r St. Etienne Son & heir to Mons. De la Tour, a French [[Refugee?]] who bought Nova Scotia of the Earl of Sterling came over into England, & making out his Title, had it Deliver'd to him, and then Sold it to Sr. Tho: Temple, who was Gov'r of it till the Restoration. Soon after King Charles delivered it up again to the French and Canada with it.

 In 1710, Col. Nicholson recovered Nova Scotia again, and the Treaty of Peace & friendship between the Queen of Great Britain & the most Christ'n King Lewis 14th , concluded at Utrecht 31/11 of March/April 1713, in the 12th Article of Peace the most Christian King to deliver to the Queen of Great Britain all Nova Scotia or Accadie with its Ancient Boundaries, which Ancient Boundaries of Nova Scotia or Accadie was to the Cape St. Lawrence Eastward on Island Breton, Cape Roziers Northward to the Great River St. Lawrence, as may be Seen by Mons. [[?Lubercasse?] Pasport to the English. And the Subjects of the most Christian King Shall hereafter be Excluded from all kind of fishing in the sd. Seas, Bays & other places on the Coast of Nova Scotia. That is to Say, on those which lye towards the East within 30 Leagues, beginning from the Island commonly called Sable inclusively, & thence Stretching along towards the Southwest. Gentlemen


   We take this Occasion to inform You that We have been extremely alarmed by one Parson Gordon's attempting to erect an Ecclesiastical Court here, but should have been much more so, if our Governor had not put some check to it, and understanding that this altogether proceeded from the Authority of the Bishop of London, and that his Lordship hath not only forbid our Gov: not to obstruct Mr. Gordon in executing of the Authority wch he hath given to erect the said Court, but hath also used several Threats upon this occasion in order to intimidate him from giving any farther Obstruction to it (as that he is one of His Majesty's Privy Councillors & one of our Lords of Trade) and having obtained the favour of a Copy of our Gov's Letter
(here inclosed) to the said Bishop of London, which sets forth some of the reasons that induced him not to admit the Continuation of the said Court. We not only earnestly desire You to make use of it, to the best advantage, to disappoint the Bishop's Intention therein, by communicating the same to

I humbly take this Opportunity to acquaint your Lordship that I have received your Letter of the 14 of Febry last and as I perceive (by some particular Intimation and by several general Expressions in it) that your Lordship is highly disgusted, that Messrs. Acourt & Dominick Langton are neither of them yet collated to any Benefice in this Island, according to your earnest & repeated Recommendations to me; in their favour, I shall therefore in the first Place take the Liberty to inform your Lordship of the reasons which deprive me of the Satisfaction of complying with your Command in those Instances, and then I hope You will entertain a more favourable Opinion of the great Regard & Deference I pay your Lords, than you now seem to apprehend.

As I did & do still presume that your Lordship always was & is so entirely well affected to the King & the Protestant Succession by Law established, that You would not knowingly prefer or recommend a Person to any Office or Imployment in Church or State who had given any just Cause for suspecting his Fidelity & Affection to the King and the Protestant

I concluded that as these Gentlemen were monstrous Tories, I should not have incurred your Indignation, by disobeying Commands that only related to their Benefit but I hope I shall not long lye under this Mortification since I have such reason to imagine that your Lordship was altogether as insensible of their Character in this particular, as of their other manifest Demerits..

My Lords
In Obedience to Your Lordships Pleasure signify'd to me in relation to the settling of Santa Lucia, I now do my self the honour humbly to lay before Your Lordships the Advantages that would arise from such a Settlement, & the Objections against it.
Advantages
1st The settling of Santa Lucia would be an addition of strength to the English in the Carribbee Islands; And in case of a Rupture with France be a means to preserve that Ballance of Power which We have hitherto kept, & which since the last peace We have already lost & are every day losing more & more. For Martinico, Guadaloup, Marygalante & Granada are all new Islands, and not above one half of them as yet settled. And I do assure Your Lordships with the greatest Truth, that to my own certain knowledge, there are double the Number of Inhabitants on the French Islands now, & double the Quantity of sugar, Cocoa & Indico produced now, that there was at the Peace, and they are still encreasing; And unless We settle some of Our Desert Island, and that Greedily, the French will be in a Condition in a few years more without any assistance from Europe, to destroy all the English Colonies in case of a War. And I myself at Martinico have heard the Gentlemn of that Island speak of it with Pleasure.

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
2d Sancta Lucia has many good Ports, particularly two, the Grand and Petit Carinage both land lockt, and capable of containing a fleet of Men of War, were they may be also carreened, and retire to in the Hurricane Months, and are as safe from the greatest Storm as in a Dock. This is ye more considerable because the English have no Harbour in any of their Colonies where ships can ride safe from a Hurricane. For even at Antegoa, which is the best of them, about five Years ago, Cap. Cha. Vanbrugh in the Sorlings Man of War; was forced to cut away his Masts to ride out a small Hurricane. Cap. Francis Home about three years ago, went down to Santa Lucia with his ship in the Hurricane time, & lay there about two Months; and he no doubt can give Your Lordships a particular Account of the Harbour. For altho I have been in it, I never was Curious enough to take a Draught of it.
3d The soil of Sta Lucia is of the same Nature as Martinico, and very proper for producing Cocoa; A species of Merchandise which the English have never yet produced and which they consume great quantities of especially in our Colonies, where every Merchant drinks Chocolate for Breakfast & supper. It is also as proper as Martinico for producing Arnatto, by both which Commodities We might have a very great Article in the Ballance of the British Trade. It is also very proper for Cotton, Ginger & Indico, of which last We make but little, tho' We consume much.

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
4th The settling that Colony would very considerably encrease the Revenue and
5th Settling of Colonies in the West Indies ought to be much rather encouraged than in North America. because they are more Beneficial to Britain; For as Dr Davenant on the Plantation Trade ingeniously calculates, every English subject in the West Indies adds to the Welth of Britain 7s 6d p Annum for every 2s 6d that a subject in North America adds.
6th Sancta Lucia, by its Situation in case of a Rupture with France would very much annoy Martinico, because it lyes a little to the Windward, and within eight Leagues of it; And Men of War at Anchor under Pidgeon Island, which is a very good Harbour, might sail and catch every ship that was bound into Port Royal, one of the two Harbours at Martinico before she could reach it
Disadvantages
1st Objection
The Settling of Sancta Lucia woud encrease the Sugar Trade of which there is already more produced than the Markets of Europe can will consume, and by consequence very much Damage, Impoverish and even Ruin the already settled Sugar Colonies. To which I beg leave to Observe by way of answer, in case the objection shall be thought sufficient, that if the 
Grantees

transcription:
Grantees of Sta Lucia be restrained in their Patent from Planting Sugar Canes it will be no prejudice to them, but rather an advantage, and be a Means of Settling the Island much sooner, because for erecting a Sugar Work, the very Buildings, Coppers, Stills & necessary Utensils will cost several 1000 pounds; whereas for the Curing of Cocoa, all the Utensils requisite are not worth 20 pounds; and three hundred Acres of Land in Cocoa can be Manured and Cultivated with less Negroes than 200 Acres of Canes.
2d Objection
The Soil of Sta Lucia is so very rich & good, that the inhabitants of Barbados, especially the poorer sort of them would be tempted to forsake their Habitations in Barbados, which are now worn out to go and settle at Sta Lucia, and thereby Barbados would be very much weakened & be the easier prey to its Enemies in case of War.
This Objection, tho People differ very much in their sentiments about it, if We may judge from what has happened, what probably will happen is, in my Opinion (with humble Submission to Your Lordships better Judgement) a very ill founded one.
About 20 Years ago, when I went first to Barbados, Col. Codrington, who was Governor of Antegoa, then an Infant Colony and not above two thirds settled passed a Law or Proclamation, and sent several Copies of it up to Barbados, that whoever would
come

And I dare presume to foretel, that whenever any new Colony shall be a settling, tho many of the Inhabitants of Barbados will very probably embark themselves in the undertaking, yet the Island of Barbados will feel no Diminution either of Strength or Commerce, but on the contrary will find an increase of both, by having the hard Timber from thence, which must be cut down to clear the ground, and which they now Annually pay the Dutch of Surinam and Isacape great sums for, and by supplying that new Colony with many necessaries, which they will have to Occasion for before they fall into a Method of being supply'd from Foreign Markets.

My Lords
The Islands of St Vincent and Sta Lucia are situated to leewards of Barbados and so near it that they are both often seen thence when the Sun sets in a clear Horizon.
That of Sta Lucia has two excellent capacious and safe Harbours Petit Caranach and Mary Gata de Durasso, one of which is easily made defensible from any force at Sea & Ships of the largest Burthen may careen close to the Shore, and her many fine Bays & large Streams of fresh Water, and wants nothing to make it as healthy as the rest of those Islands but clearing up the Ground from the Timber Trees & Unerwood.
Both the Islands abound with the best of Timbers much wanted in Our Island for building Houses Mills & all such like necessary Works for our Plantations and for frames of small Sloops which are much used in those Parts & employ many Vessels a Year in fetching those Commodities thence, & (if I am not much mistaken) considerable Quantities of Turtle for the Subsistance of Our Inhabitants & of Traffick sent for Great Britain for Dying. All which Timbers We must otherwise be oblig'd to Our Neighbours for & send our ready Cash down to Isa Cape to purchase much worse then what We have growing of our own and at so small a Distance
They

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
They were till the late Peace possessed by the Native Indians & Negroes which run off in Boats & other Vessels from the adjacent Islands, and have always with Us been reputed Part of the British Dominions, till we were surpriz'd with many & often repeated Reports that the French were setled on Sta Lucia with the three hundred Families were building Houses were clearing & planting Ground with Sugar Canes, and at last that they had erected a Fort or Battery with several Pieces of Cannon & the French Arms flying thereon, pretending a Right thereof as they give out from a Grant of the British Crown of Sta Lucia in lieu of that Part of St Christophers which was given up by the French to the English at the Conclusion of the last Peace.
A little before my leaving Barbados (which was the beginning of August 1719) We had a Report that the French with a considerable armd Force had attempted to take & carry off the Negroes from St Vincent but were repulsd with Loss by the Desperateness of the Negroes, who had kill'd many their Wives & Children to prevent their falling into the French Hands & declar'd themselves under English Subjection & fought under their Colours.
And from Sta Lucia We understood that a New York Privateer being arriv'd at that Island & having receiv'd some Affront or Disgust from the French settld thereon landed his Men haul'd down the French Colours
which

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
which were flying, nail'd up their Cannon & took away their Stories of Ammunition, And We farther heard that the Governor f Martinique had given a Commission to a French Gentleman to be Governor of Sta Lucia which is a very fine Soil for producing Cocoa which would be of very considerable Advantage to the English Crown & no prejudice to any our Settlements having no Plantations that produce that desirable Nutt.
We have likewise heard that the French have planted Tobacco at St Vincent and no Doubt that Island will produce considerable Quantities of that Weed if thoroughly cultivated the first Produce of Barbadoes & other the Caribbee Islands at their first Settlement consisting mostly in that Commodity which by the Improvement of the French I will not presume to tell your Lordship how detrimental twould be to the English Customs.
The Harbours of Sta Lucia have been of so great an Advantage to Barbadoes that in the Months of August & September when We expect our Changes of Wind or Hurricanes Vessels have gone down thither & lain as secure as in a Mill Pond for the Verity of which I must refer You to Capt Hume of his Majesty's Ship the Scarborough & it may be of mighty Service in careening His Majesty's Ships for which We have had Conveniences at Barbadoes & may prevent their going so far down to leward as Antegoa for that Service wch will be a means to keep em upon their own Station.

Paris October 28th 1719. N.S.
Sir
I have already acknowledged by the common post [[?]] this day the Receipt of their Excys. orders, signified to me in your Letter of the 6th Instant, OS, relating to the Island of Sancta Lucia, reserving myself till the dispatch of the present Courier, to give you an account of what [[?]] I have already made in obedience to their Excys. Command.
Upon receipt of your Letter I immediately waited upon the Earl of Stairs, who was of the opinion with me that it would be very proper to lay hold of the first occasion [[?]] discourse to mention this Matter to the Abbé Dubois, not as a formal complaint, but as a Report to which we [[?]]uld not possibly give any Credit, his Majesty's title to the said Island of Santa Lucia being so notoriously [[?]]own, and the friendship of the two nations at this time established upon so firme a footing.
In persuance of this resolution, the Abbé Dubois coming last night to my Lodgings, I mentioned the matter to himin the termes agreed on, but he absolutely denyed as this Court had ever entertained a thought of that
nature

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
nature, adding that if they imagined they had any pretentions to that Island I might depend upon it they would proceed by making their application to his Majesty for redress and not by acts of open hostility.
He acknowledged that there might be preparations making at Martinico, but that they were to be imployed against the Spaniards only, to which I did not think proper to make any other reply but that I allwais believ'd the Regent had too much honour, and too much sense, to allow of any expedition against the territorys of so good and necessary an Ally, as his Majesty.
Tho' I confess I cannot help thinking that England Looses by everything that France takes from the Spanish which may perhaps be worth consideration, when ever we shall be so happy as to conclude a general peace upon the plan of the quadruple alliance, and Considering the succes of his Majestys negotiations in the North, as well as the progress, which the armes of his allies have made in the South, one may reasonably hope this event cannot be very Distant.
Meanwhile tis pretty evident that France is reso[[?]] to lay hold of all the advantages the present situation
of

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
of affairs can furnish her with, and if we do not [[?]]me Measure follow her example, we shall in all probability find ourselves upon a worse foot at the conclusion of the peace than we were at the beginning of the war which I mean more particularly with respect to the payment of our Debts.
Tho' I confess considering the progress the French have made and are still making in enlarging their Territorys in America, it highly behouves us to think of strengthing ours by the most effectual Meanes, at Least the two Extremities to the North and south of the American continent, and the last of this might perhaps be best done by securing the fort of St. Augustin, which the Lords Commissioners for trade and Pantations took the Liberty to propose to their Excys. in the representation that accompanyed the Draught of My Instructions.
But to return to Santa Lucia, tho I believe we have nothing to apprehend on that side from this court [[?]]ces I shall continue to get the best Information I can of the French proceedings in those parts, and I hope their Excys. will approve of what I have done in the execution of their orders, in as much as the Abbé Dubois answer may be in some measure be accompeted a renunciation of the French pretentions to the Sd Island.

My Lords,
On the 13th Instant I waited on my Lord Stairs and Lord Stanhope to a Conference with the Marechal d'Etrées and the abbé DuBois, at which the Regent was present; the Subject of it was to be about Sta Lucia. The Marechal d'Etrées undertook to prove the Right and Title of the French to that Island from several Papers, part of which he read, but indeed in so very broken and confused a manner, that the Regent himself could not but take some notice of it; However the substance of what the Maréchal pretended to prove was that the French were as early as the English in discovering the Caribbee Islands, that the French West India Company had a Patent from Lewis the XIII in the Year 1627 for settling at St. Christophers and Barbados, that there had been Eight French Governours successively on Sta Lucia, from the Year 1650 to 1664 when some English came and dispossessed the French; He read the Capitulation made between the English and French upon that occasion, which was in common form, and he said that Enterprize of the English was made in time of Peace and

The Marechal added to this, that the English who had in that manner taken possession of Sta Lucia being sensible they had done wrong, sent Deputys the Year after to Martinico, where those Deputys publickly acknowledged before the Governour and Council of that Island the Right of the French to Sta Lucia, and condemned their own Enterprize and in consequence of this the English did immediately quitt Sta Lucia. But the argument the Marechal chiefly insisted on, and which the Regent himself seemed to give most countenance to was that by the 12th Article of the Treaty of Breda the King of Great Britain was to restore to the French all they were in possession of before 1665, and as they were before that time in possession of Sta Lucia, it belonged to them by Virtue of th[[?]] Treaty. I shall not trouble your Lordships with the particulars of what was said on our side in support of His Majesty's Right to Sta Lucia and in answer to the pretensions of the French, because it was chiefly taken from the several papers in
Your

It was urged by my Lords Stairs and Stanhope that since it appeared even by the French accounts that We had always contested our Right to the Island of Sta Lucia they could not by any pretence justifie their taking possession of it, in the manner they have lately done; and this was pressed with so much reason that the Regent owned it would be but just the French Colony lately sent there should be withdrawn, and He promised Orders should be Dispatched to this Effect. My Lords,
In obedience to your Lordps Pleasure signified in som Queries touching Sta Lucia, I do my self the honour of acquainting your Lordps that the following particulars are all  that I can positively say on that Subject.
In the year 1703 I was a shoar on that Island; In the year 1711 I was twice at it, and a shore on it, after the Cessation of Arms & before the Treaty of Utrecht I was also ashore on it and I am well assured that there was not at any of those times any manner of settlement, either of English or French, no part of the Land manured, nor so much as one single House, Hut or Habitation, excepting those of the aforesaid Indians, & Negroes which have run away at times from Barbados.
I was also frequently ashore since the Treaty of Utrecht, & observed that the French as well as the English sent several small Sloops to catch turtle & cut timber for their respective adjacent Colonies & that the Woodcutters, and Fishermen, English & French, made small Huts for their own & their Negroes shelter

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
1st Query Whether any English were settled on Sta Lucia in the years 1664, 65, 66, 67, & 68
Answer. I have always heard that some of those years (I believe about 65) my Lord Willoughby of Parham then Governor of Barbados, settled that Island, with some of the Inhabitants of Barbados, who proving sickly, became a pray to the Native Indians, who surprized & destroyed them all.
2nd Query. Whether any French were settled there, in those Years?
Answer. I could never find that any French settled there in those Years, or at any other time, and I verily believe, they never did.
3rd Query. Whether the French Comissrs appointed by the Governor of Martinico, to treat with those appointed by Sr. Thomas Wheeler & Col. Stapleton concerning St Xtophers, & other Matters in Consequence of the Treaty of Breda, did make any Demand about St Lucia?
Answer. I never heard, they did.
4th Query. Whether any French or English were settled on that Island, at the time of the Treaty of Ryswick?
5th Query. Or, whether there was any such Settlemt by the Subjects of either Nation, during the last War, from 1701 to the Treaty of Utrecht, or at the time of the making of that Treaty?

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
Answer. I liv'd at Barbados, & was a Member of the Council during the whole time mentioned in the forgoing Treaties, & can say, to the best of my Knowledge, that there was not one single Settlement made thereon, & this Allegation may be provd. Mr. Gordon & many others, whose Curiosity & Business often led them to Sta Lucia, within the Space of time beforementioned.
Tis true, We have in all times, had people there, cutting Timber & dying Wood, who built some small Hutts to defend themselves against the Weather, till they could load their Vessels, wch Hutts they afterward left, but never attempted to clear the Land or break the Ground or do any thing that look'd like a Settlement. Tis probable, that the French might privily by Stealth do the same.
But to put this Matter out of any Dispute & show that the Crown of England, by that time, claim'd the Jurisdiction of that Island. Col. Steed who was Governor of Barbados, in Reign of King James the 2nd did, at that [[?]] upon a Report that the French had built some little Hutts in Sta Lucia, repair thither having first destroy'd those Hutts, tho I never heard he found one French Man upon the Island, fixed the King of England's Standard in the most publick places; And it was not known, that the French made any Complaint or objected against this Trnsaction.
Upon another Rumour that the French had taken possession of this
Island

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
Island, King William, of Glorious Memory, sent his Commands to the late Lord Grey, then Govr of the Island, immediately to dispossess them, & on the Letter writ upon that Occasion, His Majesty was pleas'd to assert the Title of the Crown to that Island, both by the Right of first Discovery, & by a formal conveyance from the native proprietors, My Lord Grey writ to the Governor of Martinico in terms agreable to his Instructions, and woud have for'd the French from the said Island, if they had been there, but it was a mistaken Report.
The last time I had the Honour to comand Barbados, the Govr of Martinico writ me a Letter complaining that I interrupted the French from cutting Wood there; to which I answered him that Sta Luca belongs to the King my Master, and that therefore I could not, and woud not suffer the Subjects of any other Prince to come there. It is to be remark'd that in this Letter, he allowd the English had a Right equal with the French, so that he pretended no more than that the Island was a Neutral place, & when I asserted the King of England's sole & absolute Sovereignty, he never thought fit to make any Reply; I sent a Copy of this Letter, with that of the Governor of Martinico, to the then Lords Comissioners for Trade & plantations.
May it please your Lordships.
The foregoing paragraphs being in answer to your Lordps Queries. I beg leave to add, that if the French be allowd to possess Sta Lucia,
and

Santa Lucia would be of further Service to the Crown, as it is a proper Soil for Cocoa and Indigo, the King having no plantation for the former in his Dominions, & there being little m[?] of the latter, If therefore it was restrain'd to these two Commoditys, it would bring in considerable Revenues to the Crown, & do no prejudice to any of the Sugar Islands already settled; But this will require the utmost Care & Consideration.

Sir,
Before I give you my Opinion about settling St. Lucia, St. Vincent, & Dominico, & what Influence the Settlement of all or any one of them would have on the adjacent English Islands, give me leave to take a short View of all the Charibbee Islds English, French, & Desart.
The English have settled Barbados, Antigua, Nevis, St Christophers & Montserrat, and the French, Granada, Martinique, Marygallant & Guadaloup and there remain unsettled, Sta. Lucia, St Vncent, Dominico, to which we may add Tobago.
As to their Situation, Barbados is the Windwardmost, & about 24 Leagues to the Westward of it lye the French and Desart Islands almost in a parallel from South to North, in the following Order, first Granada & about fifteen Leagues from it St Vincent; next St Lucia about 7 Leagues; next Martinique about 8 Leagues; next Domenico about 7 Leagues; next Marygallant a little to Windward about ten Leagues; and next Guadaloup a little to
Leeward

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
Leeward about 14 Leagues distance, & to Leeward thereof and four English Leeward Islands. As to their Strength the English French are almost equal, and the French already make almost as much Sugar and more Indico than the English, besides a vast Quantity of Cocoa Nuttes made in Martinique, of which the Crown of France has already experienced so much Advantage that about two Years ago, the Regent by an Arrêt has prohibited the erecting any new Sugar Works at Martinique, and directed all the new Ground to be imployed in Cocoa Gardens.
Martinique is about three Times as big as Barbados & not near half settled. Guadaloup about three Times as big as Antigua & not settled, & Granada & Marygallant about the bigness of Nevis & St. Christopher, & not above 1/4 settled; Whereas there is but very little addition except St. Christophers & Antigua to be made to the English Strength, and only speedy & timely Care be taken to preserve a Balance in the Charibbee Islands, by some new English Settlement, the French will in a few Years more be able (in Case of a War) to dislodge the English and drive them entirely out from there.
The

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
The only Objections, that I ever heard against settling any new Island, were these, That such a Settlement will be prejudicial to & interfere with the Interest of the other Islands, by making too much Sugar & by draining them of the Inhabitts. As to the formers, it is in my poor Opinion, an Objection of so great Weight that it ought to be so far consider'd, as to prevail so that no new Manufacture of such a Commodity should be erected, which is already & is likely to continue a Glut at all the Markets of Europe. But if in the Charter for Settlement there be a prohibition to plant Sugar Canes (as the planting Tobacco is prohibited in England) that Objection is remov'd, and as to the second about draining the other Islands of their Inhabitants, I have liv'd twenty years in Barbados the most considerable of them & am fully convinc'd, that very few of the Substantial Inhabitants would leave it, or if they did, we should always find as we always have found three coming with Intention to settle for one that can find the Opportunity of doing it, and I am persuaded that nothing could give greater Joy to the People of Barbados, than the having an English Settlement between them & the French, which Sta Lucia woud be, and which is by far the most beneficial
and

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
and most practicable Settlement we can undertake for many Reasons, but especially the following.
1st: It is the best Land, has most Rivers & the Soil is of the very same Nature with that of Martinique, & would in process of time, produce Cocoa enough to supply all England.
2dly: It has the best Harbours & natural Basons or Careening Places. &
3dly: It has some little Islands & Peninsulas at the Entrance of the best Harbour which are capable of being made almost Impregnable.
4thly: In Case of a War, its situation being about 8 Leagues from Martinique and little to Windward of their Ports, it lies in the Road to take their Merchant Ships & retake those taken to Windward of Barbados, which are usually brought down that Channel, & lies near enough to Barbados to receive Succour upon any attack.
Nor woud it be any Discouragement to the undertakers of the Settlement to be prohibited the making of Sugar, because Cocoa is equally profitable and it
woud

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [2], 1717-1722
transcription:
would be a means of settling the Island sooner & cheaper for the same Number of Negroes that are required to manage 100 acres in Canes will suffice to manage 300 acres in Cocoa Gardens. Besides erecting Sugar Works, Mills, Coppers, Stills, &cas are very expensive & require a large Stock, and the caring of Cocoa is done with little Trouble & insignificant Expence.
St Vincent is smaller than Sta Lucia, more mountainous & inhabited by about 1500 Negroes & 1000 Indians, & not so good a Ground nor so good Harbours, tho it has some pretty good ones & is well water'd.
Tobago lies furthest from the French & could be settled with the greatest Security & ease, is the largest of them all, but we have a Notion that it belongs to the Duke of Courland, or some German Prince & I believe the Soil is not so natural for Cocoa, but it is not improbable but that it may produce some like that made at Trindado a Spanish Island in the same Latitude directly to Leeward of it.
Domenico is very moutainous, a good soil & well watered with many good Harbours about it, but as it is situation in the Centre between Martinique, Guadaloup & Marygallant, it will be absolutely impossible for the English to maintain it in case of a War.

To their Excellencies the Lords Justice,

May it please Your Excellencies

We have lately receiv’d a Letter from Mr Thomas Wier dated at Sta Lucia, the 20th June last, a Copy of which is hereunto annex’d wherein he informs us, that he had been at Martinique two Days before, where the French were then fitting out Twenty Sloops, who were to sail with Six Men of War, lately arriv’d there from France for St Vincents, One of the Islands under the Government of Barbadoes in Order to endeavour to get off the Negroes there, which are in Number about 4000. And in Case they shou’d have Success in this Attempt they intended to go with the said Negroes to attack St Domingo on Hispaniola. That the French were likewise going to make a Settlement at St Lucia which is also one of the Islands under the Government of Barbadoes, were sending all manner of Tradesmen & Materials for building a fort there, and that one Monsieur Martin, who is appointed Governor of that Isl[[?]] was daily expected with two large Ships full of families to settle there. The said Mr. Wier being since arriv’d here, We have discours’d with him and he has confirm’d to Us, what he wrote in his Letter and added that before he left

In prosecution however of the foresaid Directions to Col. And as it appears to us by the several papers beforemention'd that His Majesty's Title to the Island of Sta Lucia is fully demonstrated anticedent to any pretence made by the French; We humbly crave leave to take notice of the great Importance the preservation of the said Island may be to this Kingdom.
Because the Wood and Timber that grows upon it, and which has been constantly fetch'd from thence to Barbadoes, is of absolute
Ne[[?]]

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [1], 1717-1722
transcription:
Necessity to that Island as well for His Majesty's Ports there, as for all private Occasions.
The possession of it by any foreign Nation might be of the utmost ill Consequence to the other Islands belonging to His Majesty in those Parts: Because there are at Sta Lucia two very good Harbours for Ships; And all Ships from Barbadoes are oblig'd to pass to Seeward and for the most part in sight of that Island.
Besides the Soil of Barbadoes and of some others of Our Sugar Islands is so worn out, that it does not now produce Sugar Canes without great Charge in manuring and the Land at Sta Lucia being fresh & not exhausted may produce such large Crops of Sugar without the Expence of manuring, that if it shou'd be planted by any foreigners it wou'd prove of very great prejudice to Barbadoes and the rest of Our Sugar Plantations.
Upon the foregoing Considerations both of Right & Interest the following Instruction was given by His late Majesty King William to the Governor of Barbadoes in the Year 1699, And the same has been continued ever since, Viz:

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [1], 1717-1722
transcription:
If any the Subjects of a foreign Prince or State have already planted themselves upon any of the Islands of Sta Lucia, Dominico, St Vincents or Tobago, or shall hereafter attempt to do the same, you are to assert Our Right to the said Islands exclusive of all others, and in Order to hinder the Settlement of any Colony there, you are to give Notice to such foreigners, that shall pretend to make such Settlement that unless they shall remove within such time as you in your Discretion shall assign, you shall be oblig'd by force to dispossess & send them from the said Islands.
We therefore humbly crave leave to offer unto Your Excellencies that Care may be taken in such manner as your Excellencies shall think most proper to maintain His Majesty's Right to the foresaid Island of Sta Lucia; and to hinder the French from settling upon it.
All which is most humbly submitted,

I.
St. Lucia, June the 20th 1719
To the Right Honorable the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantaations.
My Lords,
Having been the 18th Currt in Martinique where they are now filling out Twenty Sloops to go in Company with the Six Sail of Men of War lately arriv'd at Port Royal with a New Intendt from Old France who brings Orders for the General concerning an Expedition to be made against the Negroes of St Vincent in which Island by best Report are four Thousand Negroes. I came from Martinique in Capt Harry's Sloop now gone to St Vincent to keep friends with the Indians and also acquaint the Negroes that the fleet fitting at Martinique are design'd against the Spaniards. I believe their Success against the Negroes will be small, all of them being acquainted with the Use of a Musket and if make any Attack must be by the Indians which done they desoign to carry those Negroes and attack St Domingo upon the Island High Spaniola. if succeed to leave the Negroes there if not at Fort Livres or Petty Guaves both which Settlement the French have been Masters of some time, they also affirm that
the

A General Discovery was made of all the Caribee Islands by Thomas Warner in the Year 1626 who took possession of St. Lucia in particular and left there one Maj. Judge as Governor.

King Charles the first made a grant of all the said Islands to the Earl of Carlisle in the year 1627 who settled the Island St. Lucia in 1635 and 1637 by English Colonys from Bermuda; In 1638 by a Colony from St. Christopher and in 1640, 1644 and 1645 by Colonys from Barbados.

In the Year 1663 the English from Barbados contracted with the Indians for the full & absolute purchase of St. Lucia on valuable considerations, as appears by a Deed of Conveyance signed by Anna-[[?]] the Babba or Chief Governor. Extract of a Grant of the Charibbee Islands to the Earl of Carlisle by King Charles the 1st: the 2: of June in the 3: Year of his Reign.

[margin note] 3

Charles by the Grace of God King of England, Scotland France & Ireland, Defender of the faith [etc?]: to all to whom these presents shall come, Greeting, Whereas Our Wellbelov'd & faithful Cousin & Councillor James Lord Hay Baron of Lawley, Viscount Doncaster and Earl of Carlisle, having a laudable & zealous Care to encrease Christian Religion, and to enlarge the Territories of Our Empire, in certain Lands situated to the Northward Region of the World, which Region or Islands are hereafter describ'd, which before were unknown, And by certain barbarous Men having no Knowledge of the Divine power in some part prosess'd, commonly call'd the Charribee Islands, containing in them these Islands following Viz: St. Christophers, Granada, St Vincent, Sta Lucia, Barbadoes Mittalanea, Dominico, Marigalante, Dessuda Todosantes, Guardaloupe, Antego, Montserrat, Redendo, Barbudo, Mevis, Statia St Bartholomew, St Martin Angilla, Sembrera & Enegada & other Islands before found out to his great Cost & Charges, & brought to that pass to be a large & copious Colony of English.

Now

title: Great Britain Board of Trade plantation reports [1], 1717-1722

Now he hath humbly requested, that that whole Region or Country shou'd be indued with certain privileges, & Jurisdictions and sound Government belonging to the State of a Colony.

This of Our Regal Authority is given & granted to him, His Heirs & Assigns. Know therefore that We seeing that pious purpose, and worthy Care of the said Earl have, of Our especial Grace certin Knowledge & mere Motion, given, granted & confirm'd, And by these Our Letter patents for Us Our Heirs & Success[or]: have first of all given, granted & confirm'd to the said Earl of Carlisle His Heirs & Assigns that total & whole Region w[th] all the aforesaid Islands, within the Territories of the Charribbee Islands, which said Islands are situate & do begin from the Equinochal Line from Ten Degrees towards the Northwards, and from thence running ten Degrees in Latitude towards the Tropick of Cancer.

Moreover We do give & by these presents have granted & confirm'd for Us Our Heirs & Successors to the said James Earl of Carlisle His Heirs & Assigns all & every One of the aforenam'd Islands both great and small.
